questions.stem: Northgate's coordinator prompt says `If the request is under 40 words, delegate to one subagent; otherwise run all four.` Lookups such as "What were 2023 rail emissions?" take about 3 tool calls, as intended, and must stay that cheap. But short questions such as "Is the 2030 heat-pump target on track?" need datasets and literature, and 18% of them reach ministers incomplete, while long requests that only restate one figure still run all four subagents. What should the team change?

options.text: Replace the word-count rule in the coordinator prompt with effort criteria and examples: one subagent for a one-figure lookup, two for a progress check, all four for open policy questions.
options.explanation: The coordinator's job is to pick subagents by how complex a question is, and word count measures length, not complexity: the 7-word heat-pump question needs two sources while long one-figure requests need one. Criteria with examples let it scale effort to the question, which keeps the 3-call lookups cheap and closes the 18% gap. Choosing effort is a judgment, so guidance in the prompt is enough.

options.text: Remove the word-count rule and have the coordinator run all four subagents on each request, so progress checks get datasets and literature and no short question reaches ministers incomplete.
options.explanation: It closes the 18% gap, which is why it tempts, but every 3-call lookup would then pay for four subagents, and multi-agent runs use far more tokens than a single agent. The stem says lookups must stay cheap. Running the full pipeline fits only when nearly every request is broad research.

options.text: Replace the word-count rule with a count of the data series the request names: one subagent for a request naming one series or none, all four for a request naming two or several.
options.explanation: It swaps one surface feature for another. The heat-pump question names no data series yet needs datasets and literature, so it would still get one subagent. A count of named series would help only if complexity tracked the number of series, which it does not here.

options.text: Keep the 40-word rule, and let the single subagent spawn the literature or dataset subagents itself when its own answer to a short question looks incomplete.
options.explanation: Keeping the 40-word rule leaves long one-figure requests running all four subagents, and the nested fix only adds agents to short ones. Patching from below looks cheap, but nested subagents report to the subagent that spawned them, so the coordinator also loses sight of what was delegated, covered or failed. The selection decision belongs to the coordinator; nesting fits only work the coordinator has already scoped.

questions.keyConcept: A coordinator should choose subagents by explicit complexity criteria with examples, not by a surface proxy such as request length.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.2 (coordinator selects subagents by query complexity); §5 The 10 critical anti-patterns

questions.stem: After synthesis, Northgate's coordinator checks the draft against the request's coverage criteria and re-delegates gaps with `Task` prompts such as `Fill the gaps in section 3.` Round-2 subagents re-read about 60% of the documents round 1 already analysed, but some gaps survive. The first pass takes about 36 hours and each refinement round about 5, so the 48-hour window leaves room for two rounds at most. Which two changes make each refinement round close its gaps? (Select 2.)

options.text: Re-delegate each gap as the exact sub-question still unanswered, such as regional heat-pump installations for 2019 to 2023, with the criterion its answer must meet.
options.explanation: "Fill the gaps in section 3" gives the subagent no objective or boundary, so it re-covers the section. Naming the missing sub-question and its criterion aims the 5-hour round at the gap itself, which matters when only two rounds fit in the window.

options.text: Put in each re-delegation prompt the sources round 1 already analysed and their key findings, so the subagent looks only for material not yet covered.
options.explanation: A new subagent sees only its prompt, so it cannot know what round 1 read and re-reads about 60% of it. Listing those sources and findings partitions the round's scope from round 1's and frees the round for new material.

options.text: Rerun all four subagents from the start in each round, so each section of the revised draft is rebuilt from one consistent set of documents.
options.explanation: Consistency sounds attractive, but rebuilding everything throws away round 1's valid work, and a full pass takes about 36 hours, far beyond the 5 hours a round has. A full rerun fits only when the first pass's results are unusable.

options.text: Let the round-2 subagents open the round-1 subagents' output files themselves, so they can see which documents are covered and skip them.
options.explanation: It would cut re-reading, but subagents reading each other's work leave the coordinator unable to see what each one used or to handle a failure consistently. Stored outputs are fine when the coordinator passes references to them in the prompt it writes.

options.text: Stop after one refinement round and send the draft with its remaining gaps listed, keeping a safety margin of about 7 hours before the deadline.
options.explanation: Listing open gaps is honest, but a 36-hour pass plus two 5-hour rounds ends at 46 hours, so the window already holds a second round. A fixed count decides the stop here instead of whether the gaps are closed; stopping early fits only when another round would end past the deadline.

questions.keyConcept: When re-delegating gaps, name the exact missing question and pass what earlier rounds covered, so each round adds new evidence.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.2 (iterative refinement; partitioning scope); §3 Task 1.3 (passing prior findings)

questions.stem: Six hours into a run on heat-pump grants, the minister's office narrows the request to UK schemes evaluated after 2015. The literature subagent's definition also serves two other briefings the institute is running this week. The coordinator acknowledges the change in its own conversation, then re-delegates the remaining literature work with the `Task` prompt `Continue the literature review for the heat-pump briefing.` The literature subagent searches all countries and years. Synthesis drops the non-UK studies, so UK evidence in the briefing is thin, although 42 hours of the 48-hour window remained. How should the coordinator have handled the change?

options.text: Write the narrowed scope, UK schemes evaluated after 2015, into the `Task` prompt for the remaining literature work, listing the UK studies already found so far.
options.explanation: A subagent starts fresh: it does not see the coordinator's conversation, and the only thing the coordinator passes it for this request is the `Task` prompt string. Writing the new scope into that `Task` prompt makes the remaining 42 hours go to UK post-2015 evidence, and listing the UK studies already found keeps that work from being repeated.

options.text: Add the narrowed scope, UK schemes evaluated after 2015, to the coordinator's system prompt for this run, so the literature subagent works within it.
options.explanation: It tempts because the coordinator would then hold the change firmly, but the literature subagent never sees the coordinator's system prompt or history, so it would still search all countries. Coordinator-level instructions shape only what the coordinator itself writes into delegations.

options.text: Write the narrowed scope, UK schemes evaluated after 2015, into the `prompt` field of the literature subagent's `AgentDefinition` for the remaining work, listing the UK studies already found.
options.explanation: It tempts because the subagent does receive its `AgentDefinition.prompt` as its system prompt, so scope written there would reach it. But that definition also serves two other briefings this week, so UK-only, post-2015 scope written there would go into every literature delegation of that type, theirs included. One request's scope belongs in that delegation's `Task` prompt, the only content the coordinator passes for one request. Editing the definition fits a change meant for all literature work.

options.text: Keep the delegation as written and have synthesis filter out studies from outside the UK or before 2015, stating the narrowed scope in the briefing's method note.
options.explanation: Filtering does give the right final scope, but the literature search still spends its hours across all countries, so UK evidence stays thin: the briefing's actual problem. Filtering at synthesis fits only when the search already gathered enough in-scope evidence.

questions.keyConcept: The only per-request context a parent passes a subagent is the Task prompt, so scope changes must be written into each new delegation.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.3 (subagent context must be explicitly provided; no shared memory)

questions.stem: Every claim in a Northgate briefing must cite its source. The synthesis subagent returns its claims as a structured list, each with a `source_id` field, and the coordinator then calls `send_briefing` to deliver it to the minister's office. The synthesis prompt states the citation rule in bold, yet 3% of claims reach ministers with an empty or unknown `source_id`, and last month one uncited figure was quoted in Parliament. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a check in the coordinator's code that runs before `send_briefing`, rejects each claim whose `source_id` is not among the run's sources, and sends it back to synthesis.
options.explanation: Citation is a rule every briefing must meet, and a prompt, even in bold, still lets 3% through. Because claims already arrive as a list with `source_id` fields, code can check each one deterministically before `send_briefing` and send failures back to be cited or dropped, so no uncited claim leaves.

options.text: Move the citation rule to the top of the synthesis prompt in capitals, and add two example claims that each carry a valid `source_id` from the run's sources.
options.explanation: Placement and examples can lower the rate, which makes this tempting, but the rule is already stated in bold and a prompt can't guarantee it. Some claims would still go out uncited. Prompt changes fit preferences, not a rule that must hold for every claim.

options.text: Add a last step to the synthesis subagent's prompt in which it re-reads its claim list and confirms each `source_id` is filled in before returning the list.
options.explanation: A self-check catches some misses, but it is the same instance judging its own output, still guided only by its prompt. It also checks that the field is filled, not that the ID is one of the run's sources. Code can make this check exactly.

options.text: Add an audit in the coordinator's code that runs right after `send_briefing`, rejects each claim whose `source_id` is not among the run's sources, and sends the minister's office a correction.
options.explanation: This is the right check at the wrong moment. Running after `send_briefing`, it finds the uncited claims only once ministers have them, which is how a figure reached Parliament. An after-the-fact audit fits monitoring trends, not stopping a claim from going out.

questions.keyConcept: When a rule must hold for every output, enforce it with a code gate before the action, not with prompt wording or a later audit.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.4 (programmatic enforcement vs prompt guidance); §5 Patterns in the correct answers

questions.stem: Northgate's licence for the `premium_journals` tool allows 500 downloads a month across all runs, and each download beyond that is billed. The literature subagent's prompt states the limit, but the licence was exceeded twice this year, costing $12,000. About 30 runs a month use the tool, some needing 80 downloads and others 5. A `PreToolUse` hook already logs each call, for example `run=8812 premium_journals downloads_this_run=61 decision=allow`. Which change keeps Northgate within the licence?

options.text: Have the `PreToolUse` hook keep a shared monthly counter across runs and deny calls once it reaches 500, with a reason pointing to open-access copies.
options.explanation: The limit spans every run in the month, so the check must count across runs, and a hook on the outgoing call enforces it deterministically where the prompt did not. Denying with a reason sends the subagent to open-access copies instead of stalling, and no download past 500 can be made.

options.text: Have the `PreToolUse` hook deny calls once a run reaches 17 downloads, spreading the monthly 500 across about 30 runs, with a reason pointing to open-access copies.
options.explanation: The hook is the right mechanism, but the count is per run. Thirty runs at 17 already allow 510, a busier month allows more, and a run needing 80 is cut off while a run needing 5 leaves its share unused. A per-run cap would fit a limit that applies to each run.

options.text: Have the coordinator pass the month's remaining downloads in each `Task` prompt, and tell the literature subagent to stop using `premium_journals` at zero.
options.explanation: Giving the subagent the live balance is better than a static limit, so it tempts, but stopping is still left to the model, and the prompt already failed twice with money at stake. Parallel runs could also read the same balance. Prompt guidance fits preferences, not a billed limit.

options.text: Set `monthlyCallLimit: {"premium_journals": 500}` in the literature subagent's `AgentDefinition`, so the SDK itself refuses further downloads once the month's limit has been used.
options.explanation: `AgentDefinition` has fields such as `description`, `prompt`, `tools` and `model`, but no call-limit field, so this setting does nothing. Its `tools` field can remove a tool entirely; counting calls across runs needs your own code, such as a hook.

questions.keyConcept: Enforce a usage limit with a hook on the outgoing call, counting at the same scope the limit applies to.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.5 (hooks that intercept outgoing tool calls to enforce compliance)

questions.stem: A minister's speech tomorrow quotes 12 figures, and each one must be checked within 3 hours. Each check involves three steps: find the cited source, compare the speech's figure with it, and return a verdict of confirmed, outdated or unsupported, about 40 minutes per figure. The coordinator now treats each check as an open-ended investigation, planning new subtasks as it goes, and handles the figures one after another. Which two changes should the team make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Have each figure's subagent follow a fixed sequence, find source, compare, verdict, and return a structured verdict that the coordinator checks has a cited source.
options.explanation: The three steps are known before any check starts, so a fixed sequence fits: each step is focused, results are predictable and easy to test, and the coordinator's check that each structured verdict has a cited source stops an unsupported verdict reaching the briefing.

options.text: Emit twelve `Task` calls in one coordinator response, one per figure, so the checks run in parallel and all finish in about 40 minutes.
options.explanation: The figures don't depend on each other. In sequence, 12 checks of 40 minutes take 8 hours against a 3-hour limit; several `Task` calls in one response run them in parallel, so the whole set takes about as long as one check.

options.text: Add a follow-up step to each check that plans further subtasks when the first source search turns up something unusual, so odd figures get a deeper look.
options.explanation: Adaptive planning suits questions whose steps can't be foreseen, which is why a deeper look seems thorough, but these checks always follow the same three steps. A step that plans its own subtasks makes each check's length and output vary and harder to test, and it does nothing about the deadline.

options.text: Give all 12 figures to one subagent that follows the three-step sequence on each in turn, so a single context keeps the verdicts consistent.
options.explanation: The fixed sequence is right, but handing all 12 to one subagent changes who runs them, not the order: in turn they still take about 8 hours, far past the 3-hour limit. One context would suit a task where each figure's verdict depended on the others; here they are independent.

options.text: Have the coordinator first map the speech's topics and likely sources, then write a prioritised plan that checks the highest-impact figures first and adapts as it goes.
options.explanation: Mapping first and adapting is the right method for an open-ended investigation, and prioritising sounds wise under a deadline. Here every figure must be checked and the steps are already known, so the mapping adds time and the plan adds nothing.

questions.keyConcept: Use a fixed sequence of steps when the steps are known in advance, and parallel Task calls when the items are independent.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.6 (prompt chaining vs dynamic decomposition); §3 Task 1.3 (parallel Task calls)

questions.stem: The dataset subagent reaches nine government agencies through one tool, `fetch_dataset(agency, query)`. Four agencies expect SDMX keys such as `A.UK.GHG.TOTAL`, three expect SQL-like filters such as `year >= 2019 AND sector = 'transport'`, and two expect a series path such as `/emissions/transport/2023`. The team already put each agency's syntax into the `query` parameter's description and added `input_examples`, but malformed queries fell only from 14% to 11%. Its only other tools are `search_catalogue` and `get_series_metadata`. How should the tool interface change?

options.text: Split `fetch_dataset` into three tools, one per query family (SDMX keys, SQL-like filters, series paths), each with its own schema and example calls.
options.explanation: One `query` string has to carry three incompatible syntaxes, and better parameter guidance only moved errors from 14% to 11%. A purpose-specific tool per family gives each syntax its own input contract and examples, and with the two catalogue tools the subagent has five, within the 4 to 5 the guide recommends.

options.text: Restructure the `query` parameter's description by query family (SDMX keys, SQL-like filters, series paths), with one `input_examples` entry for each family.
options.explanation: Parameter descriptions and `input_examples` are the documented fix for wrong formats, so this is the textbook move, but the team has already added both and errors barely moved. Regrouping the same guidance still leaves one `query` string for three formats. Better parameter guidance fits a tool whose input has one format that was explained badly.

options.text: Split `fetch_dataset` into nine tools, one per agency, each with its own input schema and example calls, so no tool has to accept two syntaxes.
options.explanation: Splitting is right, but agencies that share a syntax would get near-identical tools, and with the two catalogue tools the subagent would hold eleven, well past the 4 to 5 that keep selection reliable. Splitting per agency would fit only if each agency had its own syntax.

options.text: Add a query-builder subagent that turns each plain-language data request into the right agency's syntax before the dataset subagent calls `fetch_dataset`.
options.explanation: A builder could get the syntax right, which tempts, but it adds an agent and a hand-off for a problem in one tool's interface, and the builder faces the same three-syntax confusion. A separate agent fits a job that needs its own context, not an input format.

questions.keyConcept: When one generic tool must accept incompatible input formats, split it into purpose-specific tools with their own input contracts.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.1 (split generic tools into purpose-specific tools); §3 Task 2.3 (4 to 5 tools per agent)

questions.stem: `load_document`, on Northgate's document MCP server, catches upstream failures and returns them as ordinary results, such as `{"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "ERROR 504: upstream timeout"}]}`. The document analysis subagent read these as document text, and 7 briefings stated that a report "contains no data on regional uptake" when it had never been loaded. Most upstream timeouts clear within a minute, but the server's 30-second limit is often hit under load. What should `load_document` return when the upstream call fails?

options.text: A result with `isError: true` that marks the failure as transient, gives the document ID and says a retry after a short pause usually works.
options.explanation: MCP reports a failed tool call in the result with `isError: true`, so the agent can see it failed instead of reading the text as content. Marking it transient with the document ID tells the subagent to retry that load, since timeouts here clear within a minute, rather than describe the report as empty.

options.text: The text result as it is now, with a rule added to the document analysis prompt to treat any text starting with "ERROR" as a failed load.
options.explanation: It reuses the error text that is already there, so it looks like a one-line fix, but the model still has to recognise a failure inside ordinary content, and a report that quotes an error code would confuse it. A prompt rule fits judgment calls, not a signal the tool can set itself.

options.text: An empty result with `isError: false`, naming the document ID, so the document analysis subagent finds no text to analyse and moves on.
options.explanation: It stops error text being read as content, which tempts, but an empty successful result looks like a document with nothing in it, the exact "no data" mistake in 7 briefings. An empty result is right only when the document really holds no text.

options.text: The current text result, but only after the server has waited 90 seconds instead of 30 for the upstream system to answer.
options.explanation: A longer wait would avoid some timeouts, since most clear within a minute, but any that remain still come back as plain text and are read as document content. Tuning the wait fits once failures are flagged; it does not fix how they are reported.

questions.keyConcept: Return tool failures as errors with isError set, plus their kind and retry advice, never as ordinary content.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.2 (MCP isError flag; transient errors; retryable metadata)

questions.stem: Northgate's synthesis subagent needs a quick re-check on about 30% of its claims. Most of these, about 80%, compare a figure with a table the run has already retrieved. The rest need data the run hasn't retrieved, and which data is needed only becomes clear as the draft is written. Each check now goes through the coordinator, which re-delegates it to the dataset subagent, and the round trips add about 6 hours to a 48-hour run. Data governance says every new fetch from an agency must be made by the dataset subagent and logged by the coordinator. Which two changes cut the delay while keeping that audit trail? (Select 2.)

options.text: Give synthesis a scoped `verify_fact(claim, source_id)` tool that checks a claim against sources the run has already retrieved and nothing else.
options.explanation: About 80% of the re-checks compare a figure with a table already retrieved, so a narrow tool for that common case removes most of the round trips and most of the 6 hours they add. Because it reads only retrieved sources, it makes no new agency fetch, and the governance rule still holds.

options.text: Have synthesis return each claim that needs data the run has not retrieved as an open gap in its final message, so the coordinator can delegate the new fetches together.
options.explanation: Claims that need data the run has not retrieved still need a fresh fetch, which synthesis may not make itself. Listing every such claim as an open gap in one final message, the only thing the coordinator sees, lets the coordinator delegate those fetches together instead of re-delegating each check, and then re-invoke synthesis once with the results, the guide's refine-and-re-invoke loop. The new fetches stay with the dataset subagent and the coordinator's log, and only this small share waits on them, so the rest of synthesis isn't held up.

options.text: Give synthesis `fetch_dataset` as well, so it can pull a fresh copy of any figure it needs to check without waiting for the coordinator.
options.explanation: It removes the round trips, which tempts, but it puts a broad tool outside synthesis's role, and its fetches would bypass the dataset subagent and the coordinator's log the governance rule requires. A full fetch tool would fit only an agent whose job is retrieval.

options.text: Let synthesis send its checks straight to the dataset subagent and get the answers back directly, leaving the coordinator out of these quick lookups.
options.explanation: It is faster than the hub, but the coordinator would no longer log the fetches the dataset subagent makes, which breaks the audit trail. Subagent-to-subagent traffic also loses the hub's consistent error handling.

options.text: Have the dataset subagent fetch every agency table synthesis is likely to check at the start of each run, so the tables are already in hand when a re-check comes.
options.explanation: It tempts because caching is a familiar way to cut waiting, the fetches stay with the dataset subagent and the coordinator's log, and more tables in hand would leave more claims for a local check. But most checks already have their table in hand and still make the coordinator round trip, so fetching more tables up front doesn't remove the routing delay. Nor does it cover the rest: which data those claims need only becomes clear as the draft is written, so a fetch list chosen at the start can't include it, and fetching every table synthesis might check adds load to agency databases that already time out under load. Pre-fetching fits when the needed data is predictable and the sources can bear the load.

questions.keyConcept: Give an agent a narrow cross-role tool for its common need, and route the cases it can't settle through the coordinator.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.3 (scoped cross-role tools such as verify_fact); §6a Q9

questions.stem: After a refactor "for flexibility", Northgate's coordinator was given all 12 search and fetch tools its subagents use, alongside `Task` and its two review tools. It now does about 40% of the fetching itself, its context fills with raw search results, and runs take about 30% longer, while the subagents sit idle on those parts. The team wants delegation back without losing the review step. What is the best fix?

options.text: Give the coordinator only `Task` and its two review tools, and leave the 12 search and fetch tools with the subagents that do that work.
options.explanation: An agent with tools outside its role tends to use them, and 15 tools also make selection less reliable. With only `Task` and its review tools the coordinator can't fetch, so the 40% of fetching goes back to the subagents and its context stays free for review.

options.text: Keep the 15 tools on the coordinator, and add a system-prompt line telling it to leave searches and fetches to the subagents whose roles need them.
options.explanation: A prompt line may reduce the fetching, but the coordinator still chooses among 15 tools, and the fetch tools it holds keep inviting it to fetch. Prompt guidance fits a judgment the agent should make; here the tools themselves are outside its role.

options.text: Keep the 12 search and fetch tools on the coordinator, and add a `PostToolUse` hook that trims each result to only the title, source and excerpt.
options.explanation: Trimming results slows how fast the context fills, but the coordinator still does 40% of the fetching and the subagents stay idle. Trimming fits an agent that should be fetching but gets verbose results.

options.text: Add a dispatcher subagent that decides, for each part of a request, whether the coordinator or one of the subagents should run the search.
options.explanation: It adds an agent to make a decision the coordinator already owns, and the coordinator would still hold tools it shouldn't use. Removing the tools is a smaller change that settles the question.

questions.keyConcept: Give each agent only the tools its role needs; a coordinator that holds worker tools starts doing the workers' jobs.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.3 (scoped tool access; too many tools)

questions.stem: The transport minister's office asks for "the evidence on the Northern corridor scheme's emissions impact". Northgate's catalogue lists two schemes by that name: a 2019 passenger rail upgrade and a 2023 freight corridor, with different sources and figures. A reply from the office takes about 2 hours of the 48-hour window, but the coordinator's draft plan covers only the 2023 scheme because it is the newer one. What should the coordinator do before delegating?

options.text: Ask the minister's office whether it means the 2019 rail upgrade or the 2023 freight corridor, and wait for the answer before delegating.
options.explanation: The name matches two schemes with different evidence, so picking one is a guess. Asking for the identifier costs about 2 of the 48 hours, while a wrong guess would waste the whole run on the wrong scheme.

options.text: Go ahead with the 2023 freight corridor, because a minister asking about the scheme this year probably means the newer of the two.
options.explanation: Recency is a plausible guess and saves 2 hours, but it is still a heuristic pick between two matches. If the office meant the rail upgrade, the briefing answers the wrong question. A heuristic fits only when one match is clearly meant.

options.text: Delegate both schemes, each to its own set of subagents, and let the minister's office skip whichever section it did not ask about.
options.explanation: Covering both avoids guessing, but it doubles the work and splits the window across two briefings when a 2-hour question settles which one is needed. Covering both fits only when the office wants both.

options.text: Go ahead with the 2023 freight corridor, and state in the briefing's first line that the Northern corridor scheme was taken to mean it, not the 2019 rail upgrade.
options.explanation: Stating the assumption is honest, which makes this tempting, but the office learns of the guess only when the briefing arrives, too late to redo it in the window. Stating an assumption fits a minor detail, not which scheme the whole briefing covers.

questions.keyConcept: When a request matches more than one record, ask for an identifier instead of picking one by a heuristic.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.2 (multiple matches need clarification, not heuristic selection)

questions.stem: During a run, the national statistics API timed out, so the dataset subagent fetched the energy-use series from a mirror instead. The mirror holds the 2023 vintage, while the API had published a 2024 revision that changed the 2022 figure by 4%. The subagent's final message read `status: ok, series: energy_use_by_sector, rows: 312`, and the briefing cited the figures as the 2024 revision. The coordinator still had 20 hours in which it could have requested the series anew. What should that final message have said?

options.text: That the primary API timed out, that the rows came from the mirror instead, and that the mirror holds the 2023 vintage, with the 312 rows attached.
options.explanation: Recovering through the mirror was right, but the result must say what was attempted, what was used instead and what it holds. With that, synthesis can label the figures as the 2023 vintage, and the coordinator can use its 20 hours to request the 2024 revision.

options.text: A timeout error for the series with the failure type, the query attempted and a retryable flag, leaving out the mirror's rows so no older data reaches synthesis.
options.explanation: It has the fields a good error carries, so it looks rigorous, but it throws away 312 usable rows the subagent already recovered. Partial results belong in the report alongside the error. An error alone fits when nothing usable was obtained.

options.text: `status: ok` with the 312 rows, plus the mirror's URL as the source of each row, so synthesis can cite exactly where each figure came from.
options.explanation: Attribution is right, which is why this is close, but a URL does not say that the primary call failed or that the mirror holds the older vintage, so synthesis would still present the figures as the 2024 revision. A plain source URL is enough only when the source used is the one asked for.

options.text: A result listing only the series the primary API returned, with the energy-use series left out so the briefing contains no figures that were not verified.
options.explanation: Leaving the series out avoids a wrong label, but nothing tells the coordinator it is missing, so the gap passes silently and the usable rows are lost. Dropping a series fits only when its data are unusable, and then the gap must be reported.

questions.keyConcept: A subagent that recovers through a fallback must report the failed attempt, the alternative used and its limits, not plain success.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.3 (structured error context: what was attempted, alternatives, partial results); §6a Q8

questions.stem: A Northgate briefing on heat-pump grants gave eleven findings in one bulleted list. One, a 30% fall in household bills, came from a single unreviewed pilot study, while the finding beside it, that grants raised installation rates, was backed by six independent evaluations. A minister's press release quoted the bill figure as settled, and it was disputed within a week. The office still wants promising single-study findings in its briefings. What should change in the synthesis output?

options.text: Group findings into well-established ones, with their count of independent sources, and contested or single-source ones, with each study's type and status.
options.explanation: The list gave a pilot study the same standing as six evaluations. Separate sections for well-established and contested findings, with source counts and study types, let ministers see the bill figure rests on one unreviewed pilot, and the office still receives it.

options.text: Leave out single-source and contested findings, so the briefing carries only well-established ones, each with its count of independent sources.
options.explanation: It would have stopped the press-release error, which tempts, and it labels the support well, but it removes the weak findings instead of fixing the flat list that hid their standing, and the office wants promising single-study findings. Dropping single-source findings fits a briefing meant to carry settled evidence only.

options.text: Have the synthesis subagent give each finding a confidence rating from 1 to 10, so ministers can see which ones it trusts least.
options.explanation: A rating looks like a signal of strength, but a model's self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated and hides why a finding is weak. The number of independent sources and the study type are facts ministers can check.

options.text: Combine the estimates behind each finding into one weighted average across studies, and mark it contested where the studies disagree, citing its sources.
options.explanation: Averaging seems to weigh the evidence, and marking disagreement helps, but the single figure hides how many sources stand behind it, and a single pilot has nothing to average with, so the bill figure would still look settled. Pooling estimates fits comparable studies of one effect.

questions.keyConcept: Structure synthesis to separate well-established findings from contested or single-source ones, showing what supports each.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.6 (separate well-established from contested findings)

questions.stem: A request asks for transport emissions trends "against a 2019 baseline, excluding Scotland". The run lasts about 36 hours, and the coordinator's history is compacted twice. After the second compaction the summary says only "recent transport emissions trends", and the coordinator's later `Task` prompts and the briefing use a 2020 baseline with Scotland included. Compaction must stay, because without it the coordinator runs out of context. Which change keeps the constraints through the run?

options.text: Keep the 2019 baseline and Scotland's exclusion in a facts block outside the summarised history, and copy that block into each `Task` prompt it writes.
options.explanation: Summaries blur exact details such as a baseline year, and a block kept outside the summarised history is never condensed. Copying it into each `Task` prompt also gives every subagent the 2019 baseline and the Scotland exclusion, which they cannot get from the coordinator's history.

options.text: Start a fresh coordinator session each time the context fills, passing it a model-written summary of the run in place of compaction.
options.explanation: A fresh start with a summary is sometimes right, but the summary here is the same kind of condensing that lost the constraints, and it drops the run's history as well. A fresh session fits stale tool results, not details lost to summarising.

options.text: Compact with an instruction to keep the 2019 baseline and Scotland's exclusion in the summary, and let each subagent read that summary when it starts.
options.explanation: Steering compaction can keep more detail, which is why this is close, but the result is still a summary that each later compaction rewrites, so an exact year can blur again, while a facts block outside the history is never condensed. And subagents can't read the coordinator's summary at all; they see only the prompt written for them.

options.text: Have the coordinator compare the finished briefing with the original request text and correct any baseline year or region that differs before it is sent.
options.explanation: A final check would catch the wrong baseline, but only after the work delegated since the second compaction has used the wrong scope, which then has to be redone. A last check fits as a backstop once the constraints are kept through the run.

questions.keyConcept: Keep a request's exact constraints in a facts block outside summarised history, and pass it into every delegation.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.1 (persistent case-facts block outside summarised history)

questions.stem: For a briefing on a partner country's 2022 greenhouse-gas emissions, the dataset subagent returns 412 Mt from an international emissions database and 398 Mt from the national inventory, both published in 2024. The document analysis notes show the database total includes international aviation, while the national total leaves it out. Synthesis reported "about 405 Mt", citing both sources, and a reviewer could not trace that figure to either. How should synthesis present the two figures?

options.text: Give both totals with their sources: 412 Mt from the international database, counting international aviation, and 398 Mt from the national inventory, which excludes it.
options.explanation: Conflicting figures from credible sources are reported with their attribution, not merged. Here the 14 Mt gap comes from what each total counts, so stating each scope explains the difference and keeps both figures traceable to their sources.

options.text: Give both totals, the international database's and the national inventory's, with their sources and publication dates, noting that the two estimates for 2022 differ by 14 Mt.
options.explanation: Keeping both with sources is right, and dates are the annotation that explains a gap over time, which is why this is close. Both were published in 2024 for the same year, so dates explain nothing here; the scope note the analysis already found is what explains the 14 Mt.

options.text: Keep "about 405 Mt" as the headline figure, and give the international database and national inventory totals with their sources in a footnote.
options.explanation: The footnote keeps the sources, but the headline is still an average that neither source reports, the figure the reviewer couldn't trace. A single headline figure fits only when both sources report the same value or the request names one measure.

options.text: Give only the national inventory's 398 Mt, the country's own submission, and drop the international database's total, whose scope adds international aviation, so ministers see one figure.
options.explanation: It names the scope difference, which is why it is close, but even with a stated reason, it settles a conflict between two credible sources by dropping one; the guide keeps both, annotated, so ministers can use the aviation-inclusive measure if their question needs it. Reporting one figure fits only when the request names which measure it wants.

questions.keyConcept: When credible sources disagree, report each figure with its source and the definition that explains the gap; never average them or arbitrarily pick one.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.6 (annotating conflicting statistics with source attribution)

questions.stem: Fleetway's investigation coordinator splits a late-delivery bug across routing, billing and dispatch subagents. Each subagent writes draft notes to the internal wiki through the wiki MCP server and reads the others' drafts as it works. Last week the dispatch subagent built on a billing draft that billing corrected an hour later; the report blamed the wrong service, and the coordinator's transcript showed no trace of which draft was used. The team wants a wiki page for each investigation, but it must be able to trace every claim in a report back to the finding behind it. Which two changes should the team make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Have each subagent return its findings to the coordinator as its final message, and have the coordinator put the findings a subagent depends on in the prompt of its `Task` call.
options.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing puts every handoff through the coordinator. Only a subagent's final message comes back, and a subagent receives only its prompt, so the coordinator decides which billing findings dispatch sees and its transcript records exactly what was passed. That restores the trace the team lost last week.

options.text: Have the coordinator write the investigation's wiki page from the checked findings once all subagents have reported, and stop the subagents writing drafts to the wiki.
options.explanation: The wiki keeps its page for each investigation, but the page is written by the coordinator from findings it has checked, so no subagent can pick up a half-finished draft. The record reflects what was verified, not a draft that changed an hour later.

options.text: Lock each wiki draft until its author marks it final, so a subagent can read another subagent's draft only after that draft has been corrected.
options.explanation: A lock would have stopped dispatch reading billing's draft too early, which is why it tempts. But findings still pass from subagent to subagent through the wiki, so the coordinator's transcript still has no record of what dispatch used and no claim can be traced. Shared storage fits when the coordinator receives references and decides what flows where.

options.text: Have each subagent check the wiki at intervals for edits to the drafts it has read, and redo its own analysis when one of them changes.
options.explanation: Checking for edits reacts after dispatch has already used the old draft, and adds rework loops between subagents that the coordinator never sees. It deals with the timing of the correction, not the path the finding travelled, and still leaves no trace in the coordinator's record.

options.text: Add a line to each subagent's system prompt telling it to build only on drafts that their authors have marked as final in the wiki.
options.explanation: A prompt line makes reading an unfinished draft less likely but can't guarantee it, and the subagents still pass findings among themselves through the wiki. The coordinator would still have no record of which draft shaped the report. A prompt suits a preference, not traceability.

questions.keyConcept: Route findings between subagents through the coordinator, so it controls what each one sees and keeps a traceable record.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.2 (route all communication through the coordinator); §5 Patterns in the correct answers

questions.stem: An engineer spent 3 hours in a session named `stops-map` tracing how `RouteCost` is computed across 180 files. The team now wants two written proposals for the refactor, one moving the logic into `PricingEngine` and one splitting it per carrier; no code changes until a design is chosen. Both are due in 2 hours, but drafting one takes about 90 minutes. A trial `Task` subagent given the team's two-page summary of the mapping missed that 6 of the 37 call sites add cross-border surcharges, which the session had found. Which approach should the team use?

options.text: Fork `stops-map` twice with `--fork-session` and draft one proposal in each fork at the same time, both from the full mapping in that session.
options.explanation: Resuming the session by name with `--fork-session` gives each branch a new session with a copy of the full history, including the 3 hours of reads that found the surcharges, and leaves `stops-map` unchanged. The two forks run at once, so both 90-minute drafts fit in 2 hours. Forks branch the conversation, not the files, which is safe here because nothing is edited.

options.text: Resume `stops-map` by name and draft the two proposals in that session one after the other, as it holds every read behind the mapping.
options.explanation: Resuming keeps every detail of the mapping, which is why it tempts. But one session drafts one proposal at a time: two 90-minute drafts need 3 hours against a 2-hour deadline. Resuming the one session suits a single proposal, or a deadline with room for both in turn.

options.text: Spawn the two `Task` subagents in parallel as planned, giving each the two-page summary and the paths of the 180 files to re-read as needed.
options.explanation: A subagent sees only its prompt, and the two-page summary is what already missed the surcharges. Re-reading 180 files to recover them would repeat most of the 3-hour mapping, which doesn't fit in 2 hours. Passing findings in the `Task` prompt works when a compact summary holds everything the subagent needs.

options.text: Open two new sessions in parallel, each seeded with a structured summary of the mapping's conclusions, and draft one proposal in each.
options.explanation: A fresh session with a structured summary is the right move when the old session's tool results are stale, but nothing here is stale: no code has changed. The summary would drop the call-site detail the trial subagent lacked, while the session that holds it goes unused.

questions.keyConcept: To explore two approaches from one detailed baseline at the same time, fork the session instead of rebuilding its context from a summary.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.3 (fork_session explores divergent approaches from a shared baseline); §3 Task 1.7

questions.stem: Fleetway's project `CLAUDE.md` says: "Do not run `./gradlew flywayClean`; it drops every table in the target database." Last week the assistant ran it against the shared staging database while fixing a failed migration, wiping two days of QA test data. Engineers still want the assistant to run other Gradle tasks, such as `flywayMigrate` and `test`, without having to approve each command. How should the platform team prevent a repeat?

options.text: Add a `PreToolUse` hook on `Bash` that blocks every command with `flywayClean` in it, using exit code 2 and a reason that Claude reads.
options.explanation: A rule that must hold for a destructive command belongs in code, not guidance. A `PreToolUse` hook runs before the call; exit code 2 blocks it and the reason on stderr tells Claude why, while `flywayMigrate`, `test` and other commands run as before with no extra approvals.

options.text: Add a `PostToolUse` hook on `Bash` that spots `flywayClean` in a command that has run and restores staging from the nightly backup.
options.explanation: It watches the right tool, but `PostToolUse` fires after the command has run, so the tables are already dropped and anything written since the nightly backup is lost. After-the-fact hooks suit formatting or logging, not stopping a destructive call.

options.text: Move the rule into `.claude/rules/flyway.md` with `paths: ["**/db/migration/**"]`, so it loads when Claude works on the migration files.
options.explanation: A path-scoped rule is a real way to load guidance only for matching files, but it is still guidance, like the `CLAUDE.md` line Claude already missed once. It would suit a migration style convention, not a command that has to be stopped.

options.text: Set the assistant to ask an engineer to approve each `Bash` command it runs, so a person sees every Gradle task before it starts.
options.explanation: Approving each command would catch `flywayClean`, but it puts a person in front of every routine Gradle task, which is exactly what engineers want to avoid. A targeted block stops the one dangerous command and leaves the rest alone.

questions.keyConcept: A command that must not run needs a PreToolUse hook that blocks it; CLAUDE.md instructions are guidance Claude can miss.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.4 (programmatic enforcement vs prompt guidance); §5 Key decision frameworks

questions.stem: Yesterday an on-call engineer spent 4 hours on a dispatch-delay incident in a session named `dispatch-lag`. Its tool results hold queue-depth readings, pod status from `kubectl get pods` and about 6,000 lines of service logs, and it concluded that a slow carrier API was backing up the dispatch queue. No code was merged overnight, but the cluster has scaled since and the delays are back this morning. She wants to pick the investigation up without repeating the 4 hours. Which two steps should she take? (Select 2.)

options.text: Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of yesterday's conclusions: the suspected carrier API, the evidence for it and what was ruled out.
options.explanation: The evidence is live state, and it has moved: yesterday's queue depths, pods and logs no longer describe the cluster. A fresh session with a structured summary keeps the 4 hours of conclusions without carrying stale readings the model would treat as current, which the guide rates more reliable than resuming with stale tool results.

options.text: Re-run the queue-depth and pod-status checks this morning before any conclusion is drawn from a figure that was read yesterday.
options.explanation: Yesterday's queue depths and pod states are snapshots of a cluster that has since scaled. Running the checks again gives current figures to test the carrier-API theory against, so no conclusion today rests on an old reading, whichever session she works in.

options.text: Resume `dispatch-lag` with `--resume`, because no code was merged overnight and its tool results still describe the service as it runs today.
options.explanation: No merged code is what makes resuming look safe, and resuming suits a session whose results are mostly still valid. Here the evidence is live state, not code: the queue and pods have changed, and a resumed session would reason from yesterday's 6,000 lines of logs as if they were current.

options.text: Start a new session with no summary and redo the 4-hour investigation from the logs, so that nothing rests on yesterday's work.
options.explanation: Redoing everything removes the stale-data risk but throws away 4 hours of valid conclusions, such as what was ruled out. A clean restart fits when the earlier work can't be trusted at all; here only the readings are out of date.

options.text: Resume `dispatch-lag` with `--fork-session`, so the original session stays untouched while today's work builds on its readings.
options.explanation: Forking copies the session's history into a new session and leaves the original unchanged, so the copy carries the same stale readings. It does nothing about their age. Forking suits comparing two approaches from a baseline that is still valid.

questions.keyConcept: When a session's tool results describe live state that has since changed, start fresh from a structured summary and re-check the live data.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.7 (fresh start with a structured summary vs resuming with stale tool results)

questions.stem: A Fleetway performance engineer ran `claude mcp add perf-profiler -- node ~/tools/perf-mcp.js` inside the `route-planner` repository, without choosing a scope. The server appears in her sessions there but not in the five other service repositories she profiles, and she is often asked to profile a new service at short notice. The server reads a profiler only she can reach, and her teammates' sessions must stay as they are. Where should the server be configured?

options.text: At user scope, stored in her `~/.claude.json`, which makes the server available to her in every project she opens and to nobody else.
options.explanation: Without a scope, a server is added at local scope: the current project, only for her. User scope is just as private but covers all her projects, so the server follows her to the five repositories and to any new service, and her teammates' sessions don't change.

options.text: At project scope, in a `.mcp.json` committed at the root of each of the six repositories, which makes the server available in each of them.
options.explanation: Project scope puts the server in `.mcp.json`, checked into version control so everyone who clones the repository gets it, and their sessions ask them to approve it. That fits a shared team server; this one reads a profiler only she can reach.

options.text: In her user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which loads in every project she opens, as a note giving Claude the command that starts the profiler server.
options.explanation: The user-level file does reach all her projects, which is why it tempts. But `CLAUDE.md` holds instructions for Claude, not MCP configuration, so no server is connected and its tools never appear. The scope that spans all her projects for a server is user scope in `~/.claude.json`.

options.text: At local scope in each repository, by running the same `claude mcp add` command in each of the other five before she starts there.
options.explanation: Local entries keep the server private and would cover today's six repositories, but each new service she is asked to profile needs the command again before it works. User scope does the job once for all her projects. A local entry suits a server tied to one project.

questions.keyConcept: A personal MCP server needed in all your repositories belongs at user scope; local scope covers one project and project scope shares it.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.4 (project .mcp.json vs user ~/.claude.json); §7 MCP scopes

questions.stem: Fleetway's ticket MCP server exposes `search_tickets`, whose description reads in full "Search tickets by ID." In fact it takes free-text questions and returns matching tickets with their resolution notes and linked commits. Asked why the depot-capacity check was added to `DepotPlanner`, the assistant ran Grep over code comments and answered from a 2019 TODO, though ticket `RTE-2210` records the decision. Neither `CLAUDE.md` nor the system prompt says anything about which tool to use, but engineers ask such questions daily. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Rewrite the `search_tickets` description to say it takes free-text questions and returns resolution notes and linked commits, for questions about why code changed.
options.explanation: The description is the main thing the model uses to pick a tool, and this one says `search_tickets` needs an ID, so a question without one goes to Grep. Saying what the tool accepts, what it returns and which questions it answers lets the assistant choose it for the depot-capacity question.

options.text: Rewrite the `search_tickets` description to say it takes a ticket ID, with the ID format and an example such as `RTE-2210`, so the assistant passes valid IDs.
options.explanation: It treats the failure as a bad input value, which belongs to the ID format and examples, when the fault is the tool choice, which the purpose and inputs part of the description decides. The assistant never picks the tool for a question with no ID, and an ID example reinforces that it is an ID lookup. Format examples help when the right tool is called with bad values.

options.text: Rename `search_tickets` to `search_ticket_history` and keep its current description, so that the new name signals to the assistant that it covers past decisions.
options.explanation: Renaming changes a label while the description still says the tool searches by ID, and the model reads both. The misleading description stays in place. A rename helps when two tools' names overlap and their descriptions are already clear.

options.text: Add a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks Grep when the engineer's question starts with "why", so the assistant falls back to `search_tickets`.
options.explanation: Blocking Grep on "why" questions forces a fallback but also blocks legitimate code searches, and it keys on a word rather than the cause. The tool is passed over because its description undersells it, which a rewrite fixes with no extra machinery.

questions.keyConcept: When an agent prefers a built-in tool over a better MCP tool, fix the MCP tool's description to state its inputs, outputs and purpose.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.4 (improve MCP tool descriptions so built-ins don't win); §3 Task 2.1

questions.stem: An engineer asks the assistant how the fuel surcharge on a `/quote` response is calculated. It ran Glob with `**/*Surcharge*`, read the 14 matching files and explained `LegacySurchargeCalculator`, which git history shows nothing has called since 2021. A reviewer later found the live calculation in `PricingEngine`, two method calls below the `/quote` handler, in files without "Surcharge" in their names. Engineers ask such questions daily, and the answer must describe what runs in production. For questions like this, which two steps should the assistant take? (Select 2.)

options.text: Grep for the `/quote` route mapping to find the handler that serves the request, and start the investigation from that entry point.
options.explanation: A request enters the service at its route handler, so a content search for the `/quote` mapping finds the real starting point in one step. From there the path is set by what the code calls, not by what files are named, which keeps dead classes such as `LegacySurchargeCalculator` out of the answer.

options.text: Before explaining a class such as `LegacySurchargeCalculator`, Grep for calls to it across the codebase, and leave it out of the answer if nothing calls it.
options.explanation: A file name says what a class is called, not whether anything calls it. Searching the code for a class's name before explaining it shows whether anything reaches it, so a name match such as `LegacySurchargeCalculator`, which nothing calls, stays out of an answer that must describe production.

options.text: Glob with a wider pattern as well, such as `**/*Fee*`, so files named after related pricing terms are read alongside the 14 matches.
options.explanation: A wider name pattern returns more files but still selects by name, so it adds candidates, live and dead, while `PricingEngine` stays out. Glob is the right tool when the task is a list of files by name or extension.

options.text: Run `find . -iname '*surcharge*'` through Bash, so the name search ignores case and covers the whole checkout.
options.explanation: `find` through Bash repeats what Glob already does, and ignoring case doesn't change the method: it still picks files by name. Bash is the right tool for commands the built-ins don't cover, such as running the build.

options.text: Show the engineer the 14 matching files and ask which of them the `/quote` endpoint uses before reading any further.
options.explanation: The engineer asked because she doesn't know, and the assistant can settle it from the code by tracing from the handler. Asking the user fits a request that is genuinely ambiguous, not a fact the code itself answers.

questions.keyConcept: To explain how a feature works, Grep for its entry point and for the callers of each class, instead of trusting files chosen by name.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.5 (Grep for entry points, Read to follow imports)

questions.stem: Two depots report shorter routes since spring, and an engineer asks the assistant when and why `MAX_STOPS` in `RouteLimits.java` dropped from 25 to 20. Grep for `MAX_STOPS = 25` returns no matches, and Grep for `MAX_STOPS` returns today's definition, `MAX_STOPS = 20`, plus 11 usages. Fleetway's commit messages name the ticket behind each change, but no comment near the constant explains it. Which step answers the question?

options.text: Use Bash to run `git log -S 'MAX_STOPS = 25' -- '*RouteLimits.java'`, which lists commits that changed how often the old value appears; the latest is the change to 20.
options.explanation: Grep searches the files as they stand, and they hold only today's value; past values live in version control. Bash runs shell commands, so it can query git, and `git log -S` lists the commits that changed how often a string appears. For `MAX_STOPS = 25` the latest is the change to 20, and that commit and its message, which at Fleetway names the ticket, answer when and why.

options.text: Use Grep with the pattern `MAX_STOPS.*25`, ignoring case, across `src/`, `docs/`, the build output and the config files, which lists the files and lines that still hold the old value.
options.explanation: A looser pattern or more folders still searches today's files, and even if a doc or build file still held 25, today's files can't say when or why it changed. Grep is the right tool for where a string appears now, not for when it changed.

options.text: Read `RouteLimits.java` and its 11 usages, and have Claude infer when and why the limit dropped to 20 from how the depots' code uses it today.
options.explanation: The current code shows how 20 is used, not when it was set or why, so the answer would be a guess presented as history while the commit and its ticket hold the real one. Reading the usages helps when the question is what depends on the constant.

options.text: Build an MCP tool that indexes each past version of `RouteLimits.java` with its date, so that Grep-style searches can reach the file's history and show when 25 changed.
options.explanation: The file's past values already live in version control, and Bash can query it with one command. A new indexing tool to build and maintain adds machinery for a question the existing history answers. A custom MCP tool fits a source the built-in tools can't reach.

questions.keyConcept: Grep sees only the current contents of files; questions about when and why code changed need its version history, through Bash and git.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.5 (Grep for content; picking the right built-in tool)
questions.authorNote: The `git log -S` behaviour (lists the commits that changed how often the string appears; the latest is the change) rests on the "Reasoning from a stem" line in docs/lesson-sources/d2.md Task 2.5; that Bash runs shell commands rests on [CCTOOLS]. The `'*RouteLimits.java'` pathspec matching the file at any depth is standard git behaviour that the lesson does not state.

questions.stem: Before a schema change, the assistant must list every depot configuration file in the service. It called Glob with `{"pattern": "config/*.yml"}` and got 12 paths, all directly inside `config/`. Regional files such as `config/regions/eu/lhr.yml` were missing, and some newer regions sit a level deeper, as in `config/regions/us/west/sea.yml`. Regions are added each quarter, but nobody wants to update the pattern each time. Which pattern should it use?

options.text: `config/**/*.yml`, which matches `.yml` files directly inside `config/` and in every folder below it, at any depth.
options.explanation: Glob matches paths, and `**` matches any number of nested folders. `config/**/*.yml` finds the 12 top-level files, `config/regions/eu/lhr.yml` and the deeper `config/regions/us/west/sea.yml`, and keeps working as regions are added at any depth.

options.text: `config/*/*.yml`, which adds the files one folder below `config/` to the 12 paths that the first search found.
options.explanation: One extra `*` level reaches files in `config/regions/` itself but not in `config/regions/eu/` or deeper, just as `config/*.yml` stopped at the top folder. A fixed-depth pattern suits a layout whose depth doesn't change.

options.text: `config/regions/*/*.yml` for the regional files, merged with the 12 paths that the first search already returned.
options.explanation: This finds today's two-level regional files, but `config/regions/us/west/sea.yml` sits a level deeper and is missed, and each new depth needs another pattern. Listing known folders fits a layout that is fixed.

options.text: Grep for the text `.yml` across `config/`, so that each configuration file is found wherever it sits in the tree.
options.explanation: Grep searches file contents, not file paths, so it finds files whose text mentions `.yml` and misses configuration files that don't. Grep is the tool when the content identifies the file, such as a key name.

questions.keyConcept: Glob matches file paths; use `**` in the pattern to reach files at any folder depth below a directory.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.5 (Glob matches file paths)

questions.stem: A Fleetway engineer pastes three values into most of her sessions in the `route-planner` repository: the URL of her personal sandbox of the service and the IDs of two test accounts she owns. In the four other repositories she works in, those values would point Claude at the wrong service, and the 119 other engineers must not get them. She wants them loaded without pasting, but only in that one repository. Where should she put them?

options.text: In `CLAUDE.local.md` at the root of `route-planner`, which loads for her in every session in that repository and stays out of git.
options.explanation: `CLAUDE.local.md` is the personal memory file for one repository: it loads in her sessions there and is kept out of git. That meets all three needs: loaded without pasting, limited to `route-planner`, and invisible to the other 119 engineers.

options.text: In the project's root `CLAUDE.md`, with a note telling Claude to use these values only in sessions where she is the one working.
options.explanation: The root `CLAUDE.md` is shared through git, so all 119 engineers would receive her sandbox URL and account IDs, and the note only asks Claude to ignore them. Project memory is for instructions the whole team should follow.

options.text: In her user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which loads for her alone and is not shared with her teammates through git.
options.explanation: The user-level file is personal, which is why it tempts, but it loads in all her projects, so the four other repositories would get a sandbox URL for the wrong service. It fits preferences that apply to everything she works on.

options.text: In `.claude/rules/sandbox.md` in `route-planner`, with `paths: ["**/*"]`, so the values load only when Claude reads the repository's files.
options.explanation: The repository's `.claude/rules/` is project configuration that travels with the code, so teammates would load the values too, and `**/*` matches any file, so the rule loads almost at once. Path rules fit team conventions for certain files.

questions.keyConcept: Personal settings for one repository go in CLAUDE.local.md; user-level CLAUDE.md reaches all your projects, project CLAUDE.md the whole team.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.1 (CLAUDE.md hierarchy and scoping); §7 CLAUDE.md loading

questions.stem: Last month Fleetway's platform team updated the project skill `.claude/skills/explain-module/SKILL.md` so its answers end with a table of entry points. One engineer still gets last year's format from `/explain-module`, though his clone is up to date with `main`. On his laptop, `ls ~/.claude/skills` lists `explain-module`, `jira-summary` and `pr-notes`, and each `SKILL.md`, like the project's, sets `name:` to its folder name. The team's command must stay `/explain-module`. What should he do?

options.text: Delete his personal `~/.claude/skills/explain-module/` copy or give it a new name, because a personal skill takes precedence over a project skill with the same name.
options.explanation: When skill names clash, personal skills override project ones, so his year-old `~/.claude/skills/explain-module/` copy wins over the updated team skill on his machine only. Removing it, or renaming it with a new `name`, lets `/explain-module` reach the project skill without changing anything for the other 119 engineers.

options.text: Pull `main` again and restart Claude Code, so his session reloads the project's `.claude/skills/explain-module/SKILL.md` from the updated clone.
options.explanation: Project skill updates arrive with a pull, so for a missed update a pull is the first thing to try, but his clone is already current. The project file is fine; it just isn't the one that runs, because his personal skill of the same name takes precedence.

options.text: Rename the project skill to `explain-module-v2` so it no longer shares a name with his copy, and tell the team about the new command.
options.explanation: A new project name would end the clash, but it changes the command for all 120 engineers to fix one laptop, and the team's command must stay `/explain-module`. The rename belongs on the personal copy, the side that causes the clash.

options.text: Add a line to the project `CLAUDE.md` telling Claude to prefer the project version of a skill when a personal one has the same name.
options.explanation: Which skill answers a name is set by Claude Code's precedence between skill levels, not by an instruction to the model. A `CLAUDE.md` line suits conventions for how Claude works, not which file a command runs.

questions.keyConcept: A personal skill in ~/.claude/skills/ overrides a project skill of the same name, so a stale personal copy hides team updates.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.2 (project vs personal skills)

questions.stem: Fleetway's root `CLAUDE.md` held 900 lines of Java and Python style rules. To save context, the team moved them into `docs/java-style.md` and `docs/python-style.md`, leaving two lines in the root file: `@docs/java-style.md` and `@docs/python-style.md`. The root file is now short, but sessions that touch only Python still carry the 6,000 tokens of Java rules, as they did before the move. Java and Python files sit side by side in most packages of the service. What should the team do?

options.text: Move both style files into `.claude/rules/`, giving the Java file `paths: ["**/*.java"]` and the Python file `paths: ["**/*.py"]`, so neither loads in all sessions.
options.explanation: A rule file with `paths` loads only when Claude works with a matching file, and `**` matches at any depth. The Java rules then load when a `.java` file is read or edited and the Python rules for `.py` files, even where the two share a package, so a Python-only session skips the 6,000 Java tokens.

options.text: Move the two `@` imports into `CLAUDE.md` files in the Java and the Python parts of the service, so each one loads only in its own subtree.
options.explanation: Directory files load only for their subtree, the move that works when each language has its own tree. Here Java and Python share most packages, so most directory files would need both imports and Python sessions would still load the Java rules.

options.text: Move each style file into `.claude/rules/` as `java.md` and `python.md` without frontmatter, so each language's rules sit in their own file.
options.explanation: Splitting into rule files is half the move, but a rule with no `paths` frontmatter loads at launch like `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so each session still carries both languages. The file layout changes; the context doesn't.

options.text: Keep both imports and cut each style file to its 50 most important rules, so the two files together stay under 2,000 tokens.
options.explanation: Trimming lowers the cost but still loads Java rules into Python sessions and drops rules the team chose to keep. The waste comes from when the rules load, not how long they are, so cutting content treats the symptom.

questions.keyConcept: @imports organise CLAUDE.md but load at launch; to load conventions only for certain file types, use path-scoped rules.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.3 (paths frontmatter); §3 Task 3.1 (@import)

questions.stem: An engineer has two days of uncommitted work in `dispatch/` and wants the assistant's proposal for replacing the retry logic in `CarrierClient`, which several of her open files call. Last week, asked a similar question with edits auto-accepted, the assistant also "tidied" three files in her working tree, and untangling them took an hour. She wants to read and approve the approach before any file changes, but she doesn't want to commit or stash her work yet. Which mode should she use?

options.text: Plan mode, where Claude reads the code and proposes a plan for the retry change, and edits start only once she approves it.
options.explanation: In plan mode Claude can read files and run commands to explore but cannot edit; it proposes a plan she reviews and approves before any change. That gives her the proposal she asked for and protects the two days of uncommitted work without committing or stashing it.

options.text: An Explore subagent, which reads `dispatch/` with Write and Edit denied and returns a summary of how the retry logic works.
options.explanation: The Explore subagent is read-only, so her files are safe, which is why it tempts. But it returns a summary of what it found, not a proposal she approves that then drives the edits. Explore suits keeping noisy discovery out of the main conversation.

options.text: Auto-accept edits mode, with a line in the prompt asking Claude to change no files until she has approved its proposal for the retry logic.
options.explanation: In auto-accept edits mode Claude creates and edits files in the working directory without prompting, which is how last week's run tidied three files unasked, and a prompt line asks for restraint but doesn't enforce it. Plan mode takes away the ability to edit until she approves, instead of relying on the request. Auto-accepting edits fits a change whose approach is already agreed.

options.text: Direct execution in a fresh clone of the repository made for this task, so the edits can't touch her uncommitted work.
options.explanation: Isolating her work is what tempts, but a separate clone keeps edits away from her work without stopping Claude editing before she has seen the approach, and a fresh clone lacks her two days of uncommitted changes, including the open files that call `CarrierClient`, so the proposal would ignore them. Direct execution suits a small change whose approach is already decided.

questions.keyConcept: Use plan mode when an approach must be reviewed and approved before any file changes; it explores without editing.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.4 (plan mode allows safe exploration before committing to changes)

questions.stem: An engineer opened a session only to map `CarrierQuoteDto` to `RouteQuote`. She has corrected the assistant five times: each fix restores one field and breaks another, and the latest attempt brought back the time-zone bug from the second. From the failures she now knows the three rules the mapping must follow, including converting `pickupAt` to UTC. The conversation is long, and the code it last produced is wrong anyway. What should she do next?

options.text: Run `/clear` and start again with one prompt stating the three rules, including the `pickupAt` conversion to UTC, and the cases that broke.
options.explanation: After repeated failed corrections in one session, the docs advise clearing and writing a better prompt. The context holds five broken attempts that keep pulling the code back to old mistakes; a clean start with the three rules and the cases that broke gives Claude the target without that noise.

options.text: Run `/compact` to summarise the five attempts, then send a sixth correction that states the three rules, including the `pickupAt` conversion to UTC.
options.explanation: Compacting shrinks the conversation but keeps a summary of the failed approaches, and a summary can drop details such as which attempt broke the time zone. It fits a session holding work worth keeping; here nothing in it is worth carrying forward.

options.text: Ask the assistant in this session to review its five attempts and say which approach came closest, then build the sixth on that one.
options.explanation: Asking the same session to judge its own attempts keeps it anchored on the reasoning that produced them, and builds the next try on a version she knows is wrong. A clean start with the rules she has learned is what breaks the loop.

options.text: Switch the session to plan mode and have the assistant plan the full mapping before its sixth attempt, keeping the five corrections in view.
options.explanation: Planning helps when the approach is open, but she already knows the three rules; the trouble is a context full of failed attempts, which plan mode keeps. Plan mode suits multi-file or design-level work.

questions.keyConcept: After repeated failed corrections in one session, clear it and start again with a precise prompt that states what you learned.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.5 (iterative refinement)

questions.stem: The assistant refactored `RouteCostCalculator`, a 9-year-old class with no tests, then wrote 40 tests against the refactored code, and all pass. In production, 3% of quotes now differ by one cent from before, because the new code rounds each leg instead of the route total. The wiki's pricing page dates from 2019, and the class has had 60 commits since. Two more untested pricing classes are due for refactoring this quarter, and quotes must not change. How should those refactors be run?

options.text: Before any change, have Claude write tests that record what each class returns today for real quotes and edge cases, then refactor against them.
options.explanation: Tests written first, against what the class does today, make current behaviour the source of truth: a refactor that changes a quote, such as rounding per leg, fails a test before it ships. Sharing each failure with Claude then drives the refactor until the tests pass and quotes stay as they were.

options.text: Refactor first, then have Claude write tests for normal quotes, edge cases and rounding from the new code, and fix whatever they flag.
options.explanation: Tests derived from finished code encode whatever it does, which is how 40 tests passed with per-leg rounding built in. The author's changes become the expected results. Tests from code fit documenting behaviour you already trust.
