options.text: Before any change, have Claude write tests from the wiki's pricing page for normal quotes, edge cases and rounding, then refactor until they pass.
options.explanation: Writing tests first is right, but the reference is wrong: a 2019 page doesn't describe a class changed 60 times since, so the tests may demand behaviour production doesn't have and quotes would shift. Tests from a specification fit new code, where the spec is the intended behaviour.

options.text: Add a rule to the project `CLAUDE.md` that refactors must keep rounding unchanged, and keep writing the tests after each refactor.
options.explanation: A `CLAUDE.md` rule asks Claude to preserve rounding but can't check it, and tests written after each refactor would again encode whatever changed. Guidance suits conventions; preserving behaviour needs a test that fails when it changes.

questions.keyConcept: Before refactoring untested code, write tests that pin its current behaviour, then iterate on failures; tests written afterwards encode the change.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.5 (test-driven iteration: write tests first, share failures)

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's review coordinator spawns security, bug and test reviewers in parallel through the `Task` tool on each PR, and each reviewer posts its own findings as PR comments. Each reviewer's prompt already limits it to its own category. Still, about 30% of comments are duplicates, such as an unchecked refund amount flagged as both a bug and a security risk, and on some lines one reviewer asks for a change that another calls safe. The review must finish inside the 10-minute pre-merge check. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Have each reviewer read the PR comments before posting its findings, skip duplicates of another reviewer's findings and reply on conflicting lines.
options.explanation: This makes the PR thread a shared channel between subagents, around the coordinator. Reviewers running in parallel can post before they see each other's comments, and no one decides which side of a conflict is right. Coordination between subagents belongs in the coordinator.

options.text: Add a cleanup subagent that runs after the reviewers, reads the comments they posted, and deletes duplicate comments and the weaker side of each conflict.
options.explanation: A new agent cleans up after the noise is already on the PR, adds a step to a 10-minute check, and still lets subagents post directly. The coordinator already exists and can merge the findings before posting, which is the smaller change.

options.text: Have the reviewers return their findings to the coordinator rather than posting, and have it merge duplicates, settle conflicting lines and post one review.
options.explanation: In hub-and-spoke, the coordinator owns communication and aggregation between subagents. Once the reviewers return their findings, the coordinator sees the 30% overlap and the conflicting lines side by side and settles them before anything is posted, so each PR gets one consistent review without adding an agent.

options.text: Tighten each reviewer's prompt so its category excludes the other two, for example leaving input checks on amounts to the security reviewer alone.
options.explanation: The prompts already separate the categories; the duplicates are single defects that really are both a bug and a security risk. Narrowing further leaves the bug reviewer blind to amount checks and still leaves conflicts unresolved. Partitioning scope fixes overlap only when the reviewers were given the same brief.

questions.keyConcept: Subagents return results to the coordinator, which aggregates, resolves conflicts and publishes; subagents never publish or coordinate among themselves.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.2; §5 Patterns in the correct answers (hub-and-spoke)

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's coordinator reads each PR's description and linked ticket, then spawns the security reviewer through the `Task` tool with a prompt that holds the diff and the review criteria. When a PR states that it intentionally removes the legacy 3DS v1 fallback, the reviewer flags the removal as a weakened authentication check in 40% of such PRs, and authors must explain the same decision again. The criteria in the reviewer's `AgentDefinition` are correct and catch real 3DS mistakes. What change should the team make?

options.text: Have the coordinator spawn the reviewer only after it has read the PR description, so the reviewer starts on the diff with that description already in its context.
options.explanation: The coordinator already reads the description first, and the reviewer still flags the removal. Subagents don't inherit the coordinator's history; the order of reading changes nothing unless the facts are written into the prompt.

options.text: Have the coordinator write the PR description and a summary of the linked ticket into the security reviewer's `Task` prompt, next to the diff for that PR.
options.explanation: A subagent starts with only its own definition and the prompt string it is given; it does not see what the coordinator read. Putting the stated intent and the ticket summary into each `Task` prompt lets the reviewer judge the removal against what the PR set out to do, which addresses the 40% while the criteria keep catching real 3DS mistakes.

options.text: Add the PR description and a summary of the linked ticket to the `prompt` field of the security reviewer's `AgentDefinition`, beside the review criteria it applies.
options.explanation: The `AgentDefinition` prompt is fixed configuration shared by every run of that subagent, which suits the standing criteria. Each PR has its own description, so it has to travel in that PR's `Task` prompt, not in the definition.

options.text: Have the coordinator drop security findings on lines that the PR description lists as intended removals, before it posts the review to the PR.
options.explanation: Filtering hides the symptom and would also hide a real flaw in how the removal was done, such as a path that now skips authentication. The reviewer needs the intent so it can judge the change, not a filter after it.

questions.keyConcept: A subagent sees only its definition and the prompt it is given; per-task facts must be written into each Task prompt.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.3; §5 Patterns in the correct answers (subagents never inherit context)

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's nightly test-generation agent, built on the Agent SDK, writes tests with `Edit` and `Write`, runs them with `run_tests` and commits with `commit_tests`. In 9% of nightly sessions the agent gets a passing run, edits a test file to tidy its assertions, and commits, and those commits break CI. A `PreToolUse` hook on `commit_tests` allows the call only if the session holds a `run_tests` result with `"passed": true`. Each broken commit costs about 20 minutes of runner time, while most nights pass cleanly. How should the gate change?

options.text: Allow `commit_tests` only when the session holds at least two `run_tests` results with `"passed": true`, so one lucky result is not enough.
options.explanation: Requiring a second pass asks for more of the same evidence, not the right evidence: two passes before an edit are as stale as one. The failures came from edits after the pass, not from flaky runs. A count would be right only if the suite were flaky.

options.text: Keep the gate, and add a `PostToolUse` hook on `commit_tests` that runs the suite on the new commit and reports any failure back to the agent.
options.explanation: A `PostToolUse` hook runs after the commit has already been made, so the broken commit still reaches CI. Checking after the fact suits reporting; stopping a bad commit needs the check before the call.

options.text: Keep the gate, and add to the agent's system prompt that the suite must be re-run after any test edit and before `commit_tests` is called.
options.explanation: A prompt rule makes re-running likelier but not certain, and each miss costs a broken CI run. The hook already exists; making it check the right condition gives the guarantee, where a prompt fits only best-effort habits.

options.text: Allow `commit_tests` only when the latest `run_tests` result has `"passed": true` and came after the last `Edit` or `Write` call in the session.
options.explanation: A prerequisite gate must test the condition that matters: the code being committed has passed. A pass recorded before the last edit says nothing about the edited files, which is exactly the 9% path. Requiring the latest run to follow the last write and to have passed closes it in code.

questions.keyConcept: A prerequisite gate must check the real condition, such as a passing run after the latest change, not that a pass happened earlier.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.4; §5 Key decision frameworks (hook or gate)

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's CI agent must not change key-rotation config under `services/card-vault/keys/`. Last week a run changed the rotation file anyway: its log shows a `Bash` call, `sed -i 's/90d/365d/' services/card-vault/keys/rotation.yaml`, and the hook log has no entry for that call. `.claude/settings.json` registers a `PreToolUse` hook with `"matcher": "Edit|Write"`; its script reads the target path and exits with code 2 for anything in that directory, and the team's tests confirm it blocks such edits. What is the cause, and what is the fix?

options.text: The matcher is compared with the tool name, so `Bash` calls skip the hook; match `Edit|Write|Bash` and have it block commands naming a path in `keys/`.
options.explanation: A hook matcher selects calls by tool name, and `Edit|Write` is an exact list, so a `Bash` call never runs the script; that is why the log is empty. Adding `Bash` to the matcher and checking the command text for the protected path keeps the block in a `PreToolUse` hook, before the file changes.

options.text: The hook covers only file-editing tools by default; add `"matchAllWrites": true` to the hook entry so it also runs for shell commands that write to `keys/`.
options.explanation: Hook entries have no such setting. A matcher is compared with the tool name only, so shell writes are caught by matching `Bash` and checking the command in the script.

options.text: Shell commands name their target file only as they run; register the script as a `PostToolUse` hook on `Edit|Write|Bash` so it checks the changed path.
options.explanation: The path is in the command before it runs, so a `PreToolUse` hook can read it. A `PostToolUse` hook fires after `sed` has already rewritten the file, which is too late for a rule that the file must not change.

options.text: The agent picked a tool the hook does not cover; add to the project `CLAUDE.md` that files in `keys/` may be changed only through `Edit` or `Write`.
options.explanation: The diagnosis is close, but a `CLAUDE.md` line is guidance the agent usually follows, not a block, so a later run can use `Bash` again. CLAUDE.md fits conventions; protected card-key config needs the hook to cover the tool.

questions.keyConcept: A hook matcher selects calls by tool name, so a file rule must also match the shell tool and check its command.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.5; §3 Task 1.4; §7 Hook events
questions.authorNote: Matcher semantics (compared with the tool name; letters and | form an exact list) are in docs/lesson-sources/d1.md Task 1.4 [CCHOOK]. PreToolUse exit 2 blocks and PostToolUse runs after the call [AC-HOOK]. The invented setting is matchAllWrites.

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's root `CLAUDE.md` loads the review criteria with the line `@~/cobalt-standards/review-criteria.md`, which points into a separate standards repository that each developer clones into their home directory. The criteria change along with the code, as when the refund rules were rewritten with the refund service last month. On laptops Claude follows the criteria, but two developers with older clones got different rules on the same PR. The CI reviewer runs `claude -p` on fresh runners and ignores the criteria entirely. How should the team change the setup?

options.text: Add a CI step that clones the standards repository into the runner's home directory before `claude -p` runs, so the `@~/cobalt-standards/review-criteria.md` import resolves there.
options.explanation: This repairs CI but keeps team criteria outside the project: laptops still drift with their own clones, and the runner gets the latest standards rather than the version that matches the PR's code. It would suit standards that never change with the code.

options.text: Paste the criteria into the prompt of the CI `claude -p` command, and keep the home-directory import for developers' local sessions on their laptops.
options.explanation: CI would follow one copy and laptops another, and the two developers with old clones keep getting different rules. Two copies of the same criteria drift; one committed file imported by both is the root fix.

options.text: Commit the file to the monorepo, for example as `docs/review-criteria.md`, and change the line in the root `CLAUDE.md` to the relative import `@docs/review-criteria.md`.
options.explanation: An `@` import with `~` resolves to each machine's home directory, so it loads whatever that machine has, and nothing on a fresh runner. A committed file imported by a relative path arrives with every checkout at the version that matches the code, so laptops and CI apply the same criteria.

options.text: Copy the criteria into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on each laptop and in the runner image, so that each session loads them from the user-level file.
options.explanation: User-level files are personal and not shared through git, so each copy drifts separately and none follows the code. The user-level file is for one person's preferences, not team review criteria.

questions.keyConcept: Team instructions that CLAUDE.md imports belong in the repository, imported by a relative path, so every checkout loads the same version.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.1; §3 Task 3.6

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's nightly job runs the project skill `/gen-tests` through `claude -p`. The skill writes tests for changed files and runs `npm test` on them, and its `SKILL.md` frontmatter reads `allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Bash`. Outside the skill, the runner's settings approve only `npm test` and `git` commands. In last night's run the skill fetched fixtures with `curl` from an external service, without any approval, although Cobalt's PCI policy bars unapproved network calls from CI runners. What change to the skill should the team make?

options.text: Add `context: fork` to the frontmatter, so the skill runs in an isolated subagent and its shell commands stay apart from the main session.
options.explanation: `context: fork` isolates the skill's context so verbose output stays out of the conversation; it changes nothing about which commands are approved, so `curl` would still run. It fits a noisy skill, not a permission problem.

options.text: Change the frontmatter to `allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Bash(npm test *)`, so only `npm test` is pre-approved and `curl` falls back to the runner's settings.
options.explanation: `allowed-tools` pre-approves the listed tools for the turn in which the skill runs, and a bare `Bash` pre-approves any shell command, which is how `curl` ran. Scoping it to `Bash(npm test *)` keeps the test run unattended while other commands go back to the runner's permission settings, which do not approve them.

options.text: Add a line to the skill body telling Claude to use only the local fixtures in `testdata/` and not to call external services.
options.explanation: An instruction usually holds but is not enforced, and a PCI rule on network calls cannot rest on the model's compliance while `Bash` stays pre-approved. The permission layer is what decides whether `curl` runs.

options.text: Change the frontmatter to `allowed-tools: Read, Grep` with `disallowed-tools: Bash`, so `curl` and other shell commands are removed while the skill runs.
options.explanation: `disallowed-tools` does remove a tool, but removing `Bash` also stops `npm test`, so the skill can no longer check the tests it writes. It fits a skill that never needs the shell.

questions.keyConcept: A skill's `allowed-tools` pre-approves what it lists; scope `Bash` to the exact commands needed so other commands keep normal permission checks.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.2
questions.authorNote: Per docs/lesson-sources/d3.md Task 3.2 [SKILLS] [AC-SKCFG]: allowed-tools pre-approves listed tools and restricts nothing; listing Bash alone pre-approves shell commands in general; narrow with a pattern such as Bash(git status *); disallowed-tools removes tools. No option claims allowed-tools restricts the tool set.

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's PCI coding conventions, about 70 lines, are pasted into the `CLAUDE.md` of each card service, such as `services/card-vault/` and `services/card-tokens/`. Platform teams add a card service about once a month, always named `services/card-<name>/`, and 3 of the last 5 shipped without the copy, so Claude and the CI reviewer worked there without the conventions. The other 90 directories under `services/` don't need them, and loading them there would waste context. What is the best way to configure the conventions?

options.text: Move them to `.claude/rules/pci.md` with frontmatter `paths: ["services/card-vault/**", "services/card-tokens/**"]`, listing each card service that exists today.
options.explanation: The rule file is right, but a list of today's directories misses each new card service until someone edits it, which is the same gap as the missing copies. Listing paths fits a fixed set of directories.

options.text: Move them to the root `CLAUDE.md`, so that each session in the monorepo loads them, including sessions in new card services.
options.explanation: New services would be covered, but the 90 directories that don't need the conventions would load them too, which is the waste the stem rules out. The root file is for guidance that applies everywhere.

options.text: Add a service template that creates each new `services/card-<name>/CLAUDE.md` with the conventions pasted in, and keep the existing copies.
options.explanation: It reduces missed copies but keeps one copy per service, so an update has to be made in every file and they drift apart. A single glob rule removes the copies altogether.

options.text: Move them to `.claude/rules/pci.md` with frontmatter `paths: ["services/card-*/**"]`, and delete the pasted copies from the card services' files.
options.explanation: A path-scoped rule loads only when Claude works on a matching file, and the `card-*` pattern matches every card service by its name, including ones created next month. One file replaces the copies, so nothing depends on a team remembering to paste it.

questions.keyConcept: Conventions shared by a family of directories belong in one path-scoped rule whose glob matches the directories' naming pattern.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.3

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's pre-merge reviewer runs `claude -p` on each PR and must judge the PR as it will merge. When new commits arrive, the job resumes the previous day's review session with `claude -p --resume $REVIEW_SESSION "Review the PR again"`. On one PR the author's 6 new commits rewrote 9 of the 11 files reviewed the day before, and the review quoted code that no longer exists and re-posted 4 findings the author had fixed and 2 the team had dismissed. Which two changes should the team make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Keep resuming the review session, but tell it which files the new commits changed, so it re-reads those files before it reviews.
options.explanation: Naming the changed files is the right way to resume when most earlier context still holds. Here 9 of 11 files were rewritten, so the resumed session is mostly stale reads and reasoning about old code; a fresh start with a summary of the findings is more reliable.

options.text: Run each re-review as a new `claude -p` session on the PR's current full diff, so every file is read as it stands now.
options.explanation: A resumed session keeps the file contents it read the day before, and here 9 of 11 files have changed, so most of that context is stale. A new session on the current diff reads the PR as it will merge, which removes the quotes of deleted code.

options.text: Have the pipeline compare the new findings with the comments already on the PR by text, and drop any finding that matches one posted earlier.
options.explanation: A filter on the output cannot tell fixed from dismissed from open, lets reworded repeats through and leaves the stale quotes. It tempts because it removes duplicates without changing the review job, but the reviewer needs the earlier findings and the current code up front. Matching against posted comments fits only as a backstop once the prompt already carries the earlier findings.

options.text: Have the re-review read only the diff of the 6 new commits, so the reviewer sees just the code it has not reviewed before.
options.explanation: The review has to cover the PR as it will merge, and a diff of the new commits hides how they fit with the rest of the PR's changes. It also does nothing to stop fixed and dismissed findings from being repeated.

options.text: Put the previous review's findings in the prompt, each marked fixed, dismissed or open, so the reviewer reports only new or still-open issues.
options.explanation: Including earlier findings with their status on a re-run is how a review avoids repeating itself. The reviewer can then leave out the 4 fixed and 2 dismissed findings and keep the open ones, without carrying the old session's stale reads.

questions.keyConcept: Re-review changed code in a fresh run on the current diff, and pass earlier findings with their status so they are not repeated.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.6; §3 Task 1.7

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's pre-merge job runs `claude -p "Review this diff" --output-format json --json-schema "$(cat findings.schema.json)" | jq '.result'` and hands the output to a script that posts one comment per finding. A teammate who ran the same command without the `jq` step saw the findings array in the reply. In the job, though, the script receives a paragraph of prose describing the findings rather than the array the schema defines, so it posts nothing, and the run still exits with code 0. What should the team change?

options.text: Add `--strict-json` to the `claude -p` command, so the `result` field holds only the schema-validated findings with no prose around them.
options.explanation: There is no such flag. The schema is already applied; its output goes to `structured_output`, while `result` keeps the text reply.

options.text: Keep the `jq` step and add to the prompt that the reply must be the findings array as JSON, with no prose before or after it.
options.explanation: A format request in the prompt improves the odds but enforces nothing, and the validated array is already in the reply. Parsing text that is usually JSON brings back the failures the schema was added to prevent.

options.text: Change the `jq` step to read `.structured_output`, the field that holds the schema-validated findings, and leave the `claude -p` flags as they are.
options.explanation: With `--output-format json` and `--json-schema`, the reply carries the model's text in `result` and the validated object in `structured_output`. The command already produces the findings, as the teammate saw; the `jq` step was reading the wrong field.

options.text: Add `--bare` to the `claude -p` command, so `CLAUDE.md` and skills no longer add prose to the `result` field that the `jq` step reads.
options.explanation: `--bare` skips CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills and MCP discovery for uniform CI setups; it does not move the findings into `result`, and it would also drop whatever project context CLAUDE.md supplies, such as review criteria. It fits jobs that need identical runners.

questions.keyConcept: With `--output-format json` and `--json-schema`, read the validated object from `structured_output`; `result` holds the text reply.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 3.6; §7 Material beyond the exam guide
questions.authorNote: The field name is beyond the exam guide. Per docs/lesson-sources/d3.md Task 3.6 [HEADLESS] [AC-HEADLESS]: --output-format json returns text in result; adding --json-schema puts the validated object in structured_output (jq '.structured_output'). --bare skips CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, plugins and MCP discovery. --strict-json is invented. The schema is passed inline with $(cat ...) because the docs show --json-schema taking the schema text.

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's nightly job asks Claude Code to "write thorough unit tests for the changed files". In a sample of 300 generated tests, 60% cover getters, constructors and generated protobuf code, while refund rounding, declined-charge branches and currency boundaries get few tests. The new tests add 18 minutes to each CI run, and developers have started deleting them unread, but the team still wants coverage of risky payment code. What is the most effective first step?

options.text: Rewrite the prompt to list what to test, such as refund arithmetic, declined charges and currency edge cases, and what to skip, such as getters and generated code.
options.explanation: Explicit criteria for what to cover and what to leave out replace the vague "thorough", so the model stops spending 60% of its tests on getters and generated code and targets refund arithmetic, declined charges and currency edge cases. It is a prompt change, the smallest fix for a judgment problem.

options.text: Rewrite the prompt to test what it judges important for a payments company, such as risky refund, settlement and currency cases, and to skip what it judges low value.
options.explanation: It names the risky areas, which tempts, but frames them as examples of what the model judges important and leaves what to skip to its sense of "low value"; leaving that to judgment is how "thorough" produced 60% getter tests. Explicit categories on both sides, what to test and what to skip, work where vague quality words do not.

options.text: Cap the job at five tests per changed file, such as one per public method, so the suite grows slowly and CI time stays within budget.
options.explanation: A cap trims the 18 minutes but not the mix: five getter tests are still five getter tests, and the risky paths stay uncovered. A cap could back up good criteria, not replace them.

options.text: Add a review step in which another Claude instance rates each generated test and deletes those it scores as low value, such as getter or constructor tests.
options.explanation: A new step with its own model call filters the output after the fact, and with no definition of value it rates tests as vaguely as the generator wrote them. Stating the criteria in the generation prompt is the smaller and more direct fix.

questions.keyConcept: Replace vague quality words with explicit categories of what to produce and what to skip, so output targets what matters.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.1

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's reviewer prompt has the rule "flag any `print(` in card-handling services", plus an exception list of 14 harmless `print` patterns that the team added when false positives reached 70%. They now stand at 62%, mostly prints such as a request count in a migration script, but last month the review missed `logger.debug(card)`, which wrote a full card number to the logs, a PCI breach. Which two changes should the team make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Replace the rule with its purpose: card numbers and CVVs must never reach logs, stdout or error messages, whatever function writes them, and flag any code that lets them.
options.explanation: Explaining why a rule exists lets the model generalise it. Stated as "card data must not reach output", the rule covers `logger.debug(card)` and any other writer, and a `print` of a request count is plainly outside it, which the list of function names could not express.

options.text: Extend the exception list with the `print` patterns behind the remaining false positives, and add `logger.debug` to the functions the rule flags.
options.explanation: The list was already tried and moved the rate only from 70% to 62%. Adding `logger.debug` would flag every harmless debug line too and miss the next function that writes card data. A list of names can't capture the purpose.

options.text: Switch off the `print` category until its false positives drop, keeping the security and bug categories running on each pull request.
options.explanation: Disabling a noisy category restores trust when the category is low-stakes, such as style. Here it guards card data under PCI, and it has already missed one leak; switching it off leaves the next one uncaught.

options.text: Add two examples with their reasoning: a `print` of a request count in a migration script, not reported, and a `logger.debug` of a card object, reported.
options.explanation: A pair of examples with reasoning shows where the line falls between harmless output and a card-data leak, the ambiguous cases the rule got wrong in both directions. Examples help the model handle new cases of the same kind, not just the two shown.

options.text: Tell the reviewer to report only findings it is highly confident are card-data leaks, and to drop the rest of the findings in this category.
options.explanation: "Only high-confidence findings" is a general instruction that fails beside specific criteria, and the model's own confidence is poorly calibrated. It might cut noise but could drop the next real leak.

questions.keyConcept: State the purpose behind a review rule and show examples on both sides of it, so the model generalises instead of matching names.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.1; §3 Task 4.2

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's pipeline runs `claude -p` to write a summary for each of the 350 daily PRs. The prompt describes the format in prose: a one-line purpose, then sections for risk, affected services and test changes, in that order. About half of the summaries follow it; the rest merge sections, reorder them or end with an extra paragraph. Reviewers say the varying layout makes the summaries slow to scan, though the content is usually accurate. What should the team change first?

options.text: Add a follow-up `claude -p` call that rewrites each summary into the template before the pipeline posts it to the PR.
options.explanation: A second model call doubles the work for 350 PRs a day and faces the same format problem with only the same prose to go on. Fixing the first prompt with examples is the smaller change.

options.text: Add three example summaries in the target format, for a one-line fix, a change across services and a migration, each with its four parts in order.
options.explanation: Few-shot examples are the most effective way to get consistently formatted output, and the prose description is already being followed only half the time. Three varied examples in the exact layout show the model what to copy for small and large PRs alike.

options.text: Add `--output-format json` to the `claude -p` command, so each summary comes back in a consistent structure with its four parts in order.
options.explanation: `--output-format json` wraps the same free-text summary in a JSON object with a `result` field and metadata; it does not order the sections inside the text. It suits scripts that read the reply, not the summary's layout.

options.text: Rewrite the prose format as a numbered checklist that names the four parts in order, with each part's heading and its maximum length in the summary.
options.explanation: A checklist is still a prose description of the format, which is what half the summaries already ignore. Clear rules help, but when written rules are followed inconsistently, examples are the next step.

questions.keyConcept: When prose format rules are followed inconsistently, add a few examples of the output in the exact format.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.2; §5 Patterns in the correct answers (few-shot for format)

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's reviewer returns findings through `--json-schema`, where each finding has `"required": ["file", "line", "issue", "severity", "fix"]` and `fix` is a string the pipeline posts as a suggested change. In 40% of findings `fix` reads "consider refactoring" or similar. Most of these are design issues, such as a retry loop that can double-charge across two services, where no single code change exists, while developers rate the issues themselves as accurate. The team lead's first idea is to filter these findings out before posting. How should the team change the output?

options.text: Keep `fix` required, not nullable, in the schema, and add three example findings whose `fix` holds concrete replacement code, so each finding states a real change.
options.explanation: Examples would be right if the findings had a concrete fix the reviewer was failing to state. For a cross-service double-charge risk there is no single change, so the examples push the model to invent one.

options.text: Add `"minLength": 40` to `fix` in the schema, so a short placeholder such as "consider refactoring" no longer passes and a fuller fix is required.
options.explanation: Even where a length bound is enforced, it shapes the string, not whether a real fix exists; the model can pad the same advice. Schema compliance is about shape, not truth.

options.text: Have the pipeline drop each finding whose `fix` contains "consider" before posting, so only findings where a concrete change exists for the issue reach the PR.
options.explanation: Developers say these issues are accurate, and a double-charge risk is exactly what a payments review must surface. Dropping them hides real findings to hide a bad field.

options.text: Make `fix` nullable in the schema, and say in the prompt that `fix` is null when there is no concrete code change, keeping the finding itself.
options.explanation: A required string forces the model to write something even when it has nothing concrete, which is where the 40% filler comes from. A nullable `fix`, with a rule for when it is null, lets the accurate design findings stand without an invented suggestion.

questions.keyConcept: Make a schema field nullable when the value can be absent, and say when to return null, so the model doesn't invent one.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.3

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's nightly test generation sends one Message Batches API request per service, with the service name as `custom_id`. Last night's batch ended with `"request_counts": {"processing": 0, "succeeded": 1310, "errored": 90, "canceled": 0, "expired": 0}`. The errored results show 60 requests rejected because their prompts, which hold a whole service's source, were too long, all from the largest services, and 30 that hit a temporary server error. The plan is to resubmit the whole batch of 1,400 tonight; results are needed before tomorrow night's run, and the team wants them without paying twice for finished work. Which two steps should the team take instead? (Select 2.)

options.text: Resubmit the whole batch of 1,400 as planned, so that each service's tests come from one run with one prompt version.
options.explanation: This throws away 1,310 good results and pays to produce them again, and the 60 oversized prompts would fail again unchanged. A fresh full run fits only when the prompt itself has changed.

options.text: Resend only the 90 errored services, found by their `custom_id`, and keep the 1,310 succeeded results as they are.
options.explanation: `custom_id` ties each result to its request, so the 90 failures can be picked out and resent while the 1,310 good results stay. Resending the whole batch pays again for work already done.

options.text: Send the 60 oversized requests through synchronous calls with the same prompts, so they skip the batch queue and finish tonight.
options.explanation: It blames the batch queue, but the queue was not the problem: a prompt too long for a batch request is too long for a synchronous call too. Moving work to synchronous calls fits a job that needs results at once, not a request that is invalid on either API.

options.text: Before resending, split each of the 60 oversized requests into per-module requests with their own `custom_id`s, so each prompt fits.
options.explanation: Failures differ by cause. The 30 server errors can be resent unchanged, but the 60 requests were invalid and would fail the same way again, so they must be fixed first; smaller per-module prompts fit.

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` on the 60 oversized requests so their long prompts fit, then resend them together with the other 30.
options.explanation: `max_tokens` caps the length of the response, not the size of the prompt, so the 60 requests would be rejected again. Raising it fits output that is being cut off.

questions.keyConcept: After a batch, resend only failed `custom_id`s, and fix invalid requests before resending; transient failures can go back unchanged.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.5; §6c Q3

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's code-generation agent fixes failing tests, then spawns a reviewer subagent through the `Task` tool and writes the reviewer's prompt itself, which often begins "I handled the null case by…". The reviewer approves 97% of fixes, but human reviewers reject 1 in 5. The team already told the generator to pass only the diff, yet 40% of `Task` prompts still explain its approach. Reviews must stay inside the 10-minute pre-merge check. How should the architect change the review?

options.text: Have the generator review its own diff before spawning anything, using extended thinking and the team's review checklist for payment code.
options.explanation: This is self-review inside the session that wrote the fix, the weakest option: the model keeps its generation reasoning and rarely questions it. A checklist or more thinking does not remove that bias.

options.text: Have the pipeline start the reviewer as a separate `claude -p` step, given the diff, the ticket and the review criteria, none of the generator's notes.
options.explanation: An independent reviewer works only if it lacks the author's reasoning, and here the author writes the reviewer's prompt. When the pipeline starts the reviewer and chooses its input, the generator cannot frame the review, so the reviewer judges the diff against the ticket and criteria on its own, still inside the pre-merge check.

options.text: Keep the `Task` reviewer and have it report a confidence score per finding, sending each fix it rates below 0.8 to a human reviewer.
options.explanation: A reviewer primed with the author's reasoning will also be confident in its approvals, so the threshold rarely fires, and uncalibrated self-confidence is a poor routing signal. The bias in its input is the problem.

options.text: Keep the `Task` reviewer, and put the pass-only-the-diff rule in capitals at the top of the generator's system prompt, with an example `Task` prompt to copy.
options.explanation: The instruction was already tried and 40% of prompts still explain the approach; emphasis and an example may lower that, but the generator still decides what the reviewer sees. Prompt wording fits preferences, not the independence the review depends on.

questions.keyConcept: An independent reviewer must get its input from the pipeline, not from the author, or the author's reasoning comes along.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.6; §3 Task 1.3

questions.stem: Harlow Mutual's claim-assembly agent loops while `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`, with a cap of 12 iterations as a backstop; normal claims finish in about 6. When the cap is hit, the code passes the record built so far to `submit_to_adjudication` as finished, and most such records pass the schema validator, since unfilled fields are nullable. Last week 140 runs hit the cap, each ending like `iter 12: tool_use lookup_policy {"policy_number": "HM-204381"}` after 7 earlier identical calls. What should the code do when the cap is hit?

options.text: Treat the run as incomplete, and send the claim to `route_to_review` with the fields gathered so far and a note that the loop stopped at the cap.
options.explanation: A cap is a safety net, so a run it stops has not finished: these 140 runs were stuck repeating `lookup_policy`, and their records are partial even when they pass the schema. Sending the claim to review with what was gathered keeps partial records out of adjudication without losing the work done.

options.text: Increase the cap from 12 to 30 so that long claims can finish, and keep sending the record to `submit_to_adjudication` when the cap is hit.
options.explanation: It tempts because the cap is what cut the runs short. But the capped runs repeat one `lookup_policy` call, so 30 iterations would only repeat it for longer, and capped records would still reach adjudication as complete. A higher cap is right when normal work routinely needs more steps than the cap allows.

options.text: Treat the run as complete if its record passes the schema validator and send it to `submit_to_adjudication`; if not, send the claim to `route_to_review` with the fields gathered.
options.explanation: It sounds like a safety check, but most capped records pass the schema because unfilled fields are nullable, so most would still reach adjudication. A schema checks shape, not whether the agent finished. A schema gate suits records from runs that ended normally.

options.text: Restart the claim in a fresh loop with an empty history, and send that run's record to `submit_to_adjudication` when its loop ends.
options.explanation: Restarting throws away the work the run already did, and with the repetition seen in 140 runs a fresh loop is likely to fall into the same pattern and hit the cap. A restart suits a run that failed from a passing cause, not one that loops.

questions.keyConcept: A run stopped by an iteration cap is unfinished; handle it as an incomplete result, not as a completed one.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.1 (iteration caps as a safety net); §5 The 10 critical anti-patterns

questions.stem: Harlow Mutual's consistency subagent checks that each claim's repair came after the incident. `get_police_record` returns dates as dd/mm/yyyy, but `get_garage_invoice`, which reads a US-owned garage portal, returns mm/dd/yyyy. Both are vendor MCP servers whose output the team can't change. Results such as `"repair_date": "03/04/2025"` reach the model with no format marker, and 2% of the subagent's date-order checks are wrong, each one a claim paid or denied on a misread date. Which change makes the date-order check reliable?

options.text: A `PostToolUse` hook on both tools that rewrites each date to ISO 8601, reading it as dd/mm for `get_police_record` and as mm/dd for `get_garage_invoice`.
options.explanation: Hooks are deterministic, and a `PostToolUse` hook changes a result before the model sees it. The code knows which tool each date came from, so it can read "03/04/2025" as 3 April from the police record and 4 March from the invoice, removing the ambiguity behind the 2% of wrong checks.

options.text: A `PostToolUse` hook on both tools that rewrites each date to ISO 8601, reading it as mm/dd when its first part is 12 or under and as dd/mm otherwise.
options.explanation: It is the right hook at the right point with the wrong rule: police dates are dd/mm, so a police date of 03/04 would become 4 March. A guess from the digits is needed only when the source format is unknown; here the tool that produced the date tells you its format.

options.text: A system-prompt rule stating that `get_police_record` gives dd/mm and `get_garage_invoice` gives mm/dd, with one worked example of each format from a real claim.
options.explanation: The model would usually apply the rule, but a prompt is a probabilistic nudge, and each miss is a claim decided on a wrong date. A prompt rule suits a preference; a comparison that decides payment needs the conversion done in code.

options.text: A code step after extraction that rewrites the police and repair dates, such as 03/04/2025, in the extracted records to ISO 8601 before they reach adjudication.
options.explanation: The model compares the dates while it works, before any record exists, so normalising the extracted records comes too late to fix the check. A post-extraction step suits formatting output for adjudication, not inputs the model must reason over.

questions.keyConcept: Normalise mixed formats from different tools in a PostToolUse hook, using each tool's known format, before the model reasons over them.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.5 (normalising heterogeneous formats in PostToolUse hooks)

questions.stem: Harlow Mutual's coverage subagent has five tools that each return one fact from the same policy record: `get_policy_status`, `get_policy_limits`, `get_policy_excess`, `get_policy_vehicles` and `get_policy_dates`, each taking a `policy_number`. Traces show 3 to 4 of these calls per claim, and on 8% of claims the subagent calls the wrong one, for example `get_policy_dates` when it needs the excess. The subagent also holds three claim-history tools. Each call adds latency to the nightly run, though cost per claim must stay low. What is the best fix?

options.text: Replace the five policy tools with one `get_policy(policy_number, sections)` tool, whose `sections` parameter lists the parts of the record that the subagent needs.
options.explanation: The five tools overlap: each returns one slice of the same record, so the subagent must choose between near-identical tools and make 3 to 4 calls per claim. One tool with a `sections` parameter removes the choice behind the 8% of wrong picks and cuts the calls to one.

options.text: Rewrite the five policy tool descriptions so each names the record section it returns, such as limits or excess, with an example and which tool to use for the other sections.
options.explanation: Clearer descriptions are the usual first fix for wrong picks and would help a little, but five tools over one record still invite confusion and still cost 3 to 4 calls per claim. Rewriting descriptions is the fix when tools do different jobs, as the claim-history tools do.

options.text: Add a sixth policy tool, `get_policy_summary(policy_number)`, that returns each section of the record, and keep the five single-fact tools for narrow lookups.
options.explanation: A sixth tool that overlaps the other five adds another near-identical choice instead of removing any, so wrong picks can rise. A broad tool suits a gap in coverage, not a set of tools that already split one record between them.

options.text: Move the five policy tools to a new policy subagent, and have the coverage subagent request each policy fact from it through the coordinator.
options.explanation: A new subagent adds a component, a handoff through the coordinator and more latency per claim, while the selection problem moves with the tools. A separate agent suits a different role, not five thin lookups on one record.

questions.keyConcept: Combine tools that each return one slice of the same record into one tool with a parameter that selects what to return.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.1 (tool boundaries and overlap); §7 material beyond the guide
questions.authorNote: Combining overlapping thin tools into one tool with a selecting parameter comes from Anthropic Academy, 'Tool use with the Messages API: Creating tools that Claude picks' (AC-PICK in docs/lesson-sources/d2.md), not from the exam guide's task statements.

questions.stem: `submit_to_adjudication` refuses a claim whose policy had lapsed before the loss date, and returns `{"isError": true, "message": "Rejected"}`. Harlow Mutual's agent retries each such claim three times, then sends it to `route_to_review` with no reason. About 90 claims a night take this path, and reviewers spend roughly 10 minutes on each one finding the lapse in the policy system. Other rejections, though, such as a timeout inside the adjudication system, do clear when tried again. What should `submit_to_adjudication` return for a lapsed policy?

options.text: `isError: true` with category `business` and retryable set to false, plus a message stating the lapse date and loss date that the agent passes on to review.
options.explanation: A lapsed policy is a business-rule violation: no retry changes the outcome, so marking the error as not retryable stops the three wasted attempts. Putting the lapse date and the loss date in the message hands reviewers the reason, saving about 10 minutes on each of 90 claims a night.

options.text: `isError: true` with category `transient` and retryable set to true, plus a message giving the policy's lapse date and loss date, so the agent passes it to `route_to_review` if retries fail.
options.explanation: The dates would help reviewers, but marking a lapse as transient and retryable tells the agent to keep trying a claim that will be refused each time. That category fits the adjudication timeouts, which do clear when tried again.

options.text: `isError: false` with `status: "held"`, so that the claim waits inside the adjudication system until a reviewer happens to open it there.
options.explanation: Reporting success hides the refusal: the agent believes the claim went through, nothing reaches the review queue, and lapsed claims sit unseen. A held status suits work that really is queued for action, not a refusal.

options.text: The existing `"Rejected"` message, plus a system-prompt rule telling the agent not to retry `submit_to_adjudication` and to route each rejection to review.
options.explanation: Behind one generic message the agent can't tell a lapse from a timeout, so it would also stop retrying timeouts that would clear, and reviewers would still get no reason. The error itself has to carry the category and the cause.

questions.keyConcept: For a business-rule refusal, return a non-retryable business error with the specific reason, so retries stop and the next handler knows why.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.2 (error categories, retryable flag, business-rule errors)

questions.stem: In a trial of a new medical-bill pipeline, Harlow Mutual's coordinator gives each bill to an extraction subagent holding `extract_fields`, `read_page` and `route_to_review`. The subagents send 18% of bills to the review queue themselves, often for one faint field on an otherwise clear page. At full volume that would be about 2,000 bills a night, while the 12 reviewers can check about 1,800 documents of every type together. Each subagent sees only its own bill; the coordinator sees the whole claim and the night's review queue. What is the right fix?

options.text: Remove `route_to_review` from the extraction subagents; each sends its fields and calibrated field-level confidences back, and the coordinator picks the bills to review.
options.explanation: Agents misuse tools outside their role: an extraction subagent sees one bill and can't weigh it against a night's queue of about 1,800 places. Returning calibrated field confidences lets the coordinator, which sees the whole claim and the queue, make the routing call, so one faint field no longer sends a clear bill to review.

options.text: Keep `route_to_review` on the extraction subagents, behind a `PreToolUse` hook that denies the call after 1,800 documents are queued that night.
options.explanation: A cap on calls stops the overflow but picks bills by arrival time, so a bill with a costly doubtful field after the cutoff goes unreviewed while earlier clear bills took the places. A `PreToolUse` gate suits a rule each call can be judged by alone, not a choice across the night's queue.

options.text: Have each extraction subagent write its flagged fields, with field-level confidences, to a shared review table that the 12 reviewers sort and work through.
options.explanation: Writing to a shared table routes around the coordinator, which loses sight of what is queued and why, and the subagents still decide alone what to flag, so the table overflows the 1,800 places. Hub-and-spoke routing keeps the decision where the whole claim is visible.

options.text: Give the extraction subagents a `get_queue_status` tool as well, so each one checks how many review places are left before calling `route_to_review`.
options.explanation: Another tool widens the subagents' role instead of narrowing it, and each would still judge its bill alone, racing the others for places. A queue-status tool suits the coordinator, which owns routing.

questions.keyConcept: Give a tool only to the agent whose role needs it; a subagent that sees one item shouldn't make decisions that need the whole picture.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.3 (tools outside a role get misused; scoped access)

questions.stem: Harlow Mutual's claim-form prompt says: "Extract only values you are highly confident of; otherwise return null." On handwritten forms 40% of fields come back null, although reviewers read most of them without difficulty, and each null sends the form to the 12 reviewers. On typed forms the null rate is 3%. The pipeline must still not invent a value for a field that is blank or illegible. What should the prompt say instead?

options.text: Extract a value when it is legible in its labelled box, handwritten or typed; return null only when the box is blank or illegible.
options.explanation: Vague instructions such as "only high confidence" fail against categorical criteria. Legible in its labelled box is something the model can check, so readable handwritten fields get extracted, while blank or illegible boxes still return null and nothing is invented.

options.text: Extract a value when you are at least 60% confident of it, handwritten or typed; return null when your confidence in the value is below 60%.
options.explanation: A number looks precise, but it still rests on the model's own sense of confidence, which is not calibrated, so handwritten fields may keep falling below the line. Confidence thresholds work when calibrated on labelled data, not as a prompt instruction.

options.text: Extract a value for each field, taking the nearest legible text on the form when its labelled box is blank or illegible; return null only if none is found.
options.explanation: Filling a blank box from nearby text invents a value, which the pipeline must not do; the null rate would fall by putting wrong data into fields. A blank or illegible box is the case the pipeline sends to the 12 reviewers, not one to guess at.

options.text: Keep the instruction for typed forms, and send each handwritten form straight to the 12 reviewers without running any extraction on it first.
options.explanation: Sending handwritten forms straight to review loads 12 reviewers with forms the model could mostly read. Direct review suits a document type the model can't handle, which the reviewers' easy reading here rules out.

questions.keyConcept: Replace vague confidence instructions with categorical criteria that say exactly when to extract a value and when to return null.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.1 (explicit criteria vs "be conservative")

questions.stem: Harlow Mutual's repair-invoice prompt has grown one rule per garage layout, 14 so far, such as "For Mercer Motors, labour is the column headed 'Time'." About 3 new layouts appear each month, and each one mislabels labour and parts for its first week until someone writes its rule. The prompt must stay compact at 30,000 documents a night, but labour and parts must be told apart on any layout. What is the better approach?

options.text: Replace the 14 rules with three or four examples from varied layouts, each showing the reasoning that tells labour from parts, such as hours times a rate.
options.explanation: Examples that show the reasoning let the model generalise to layouts it hasn't seen, which per-garage rules can't do: each rule covers one layout, so each of the 3 new layouts a month fails until its rule exists. A few varied examples also keep the prompt compact.

options.text: Replace the 14 rules with three or four examples from the four highest-volume garages, each showing the labour and parts values extracted from that garage's own invoice.
options.explanation: Examples are the right tool, but four from the busiest garages with no reasoning teach those layouts, not how to tell labour from parts, so new layouts would still fail. Examples drawn from one kind of input suit a pipeline whose inputs really are that uniform.

options.text: Keep the 14 rules, and add a classifier that detects each invoice's garage and loads only that garage's rule into the prompt for that invoice.
options.explanation: A classifier makes each rule load only where it applies, but a new garage still has no rule, so the first-week failures stay. It adds a component without fixing why new layouts fail.

options.text: Keep the 14 rules, and send each invoice from a garage that has no rule yet to the 12 reviewers until someone writes that garage's rule.
options.explanation: Sending unknown layouts to review hides the failures at the reviewers' cost, and the rule list keeps growing. Review suits documents the model can't handle, not ones it could read with better examples.

questions.keyConcept: When each new input pattern needs its own rule, use a few varied examples with reasoning so the model generalises to unseen patterns.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.2 (examples generalise to new patterns)

questions.stem: In 2% of Harlow Mutual's claim-form extractions, the vehicle's VIN lands in `policy_number`. Both are string fields in the extraction schema, so the output parses, but adjudication then fails to find the policy. An engineer proposes turning on `strict: true` for the extraction tool to stop this. Policy numbers are `HM-` followed by 6 digits, VINs are 17 characters, and the `policy_number` field description reads only "The policy number." How should the architect respond? (Select 2.)

options.text: Add validator checks that `policy_number` is `HM-` plus 6 digits and `vin` is 17 characters, and retry a failure with the document, the record and the specific error.
options.explanation: Strict schemas remove syntax errors, not semantic ones, and a VIN in `policy_number` is a valid string. Format checks in the validator catch the 2%, and a retry with the document, the failed record and the specific error lets the model put each value where it belongs.

options.text: Rewrite the `policy_number` and `vin` field descriptions to state each format with an example, such as `HM-204381`, and where each appears on the claim form.
options.explanation: Formats and examples belong in each field's description: "The policy number." gives the model nothing to tell a 17-character VIN from `HM-` plus 6 digits. Clear descriptions make the swap less likely in the first place, while the validator catches what still slips through.

options.text: Accept the proposal, because `strict: true` makes the tool input match the schema, so a VIN can no longer be placed in `policy_number`.
options.explanation: Strict mode guarantees the output matches the schema's shape, and the swapped records already do, since both fields are strings. It would be the right setting if records failed to parse, which these don't.

options.text: Move claim-form extraction to a larger model, which is less likely to confuse two long identifiers on a crowded, partly handwritten form.
options.explanation: A larger model may confuse the fields less often, but the cause is a description that gives no format and a validator that checks none. Fix the prompt and the checks first; move to a bigger model only when those stop helping.

options.text: Mark `policy_number` and `vin` as required in the extraction schema, so that the model has to fill each one from its own box on the form.
options.explanation: Both fields are already filled in the swapped records; required only says a field must be present, not which value belongs in it. Required fields suit values every document holds, and they can push the model to invent one when it is missing.

questions.keyConcept: Strict schemas stop syntax errors, not values in the wrong field; catch those with validator checks, retry feedback and clear field formats.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.4 (semantic vs syntax errors, retry with error feedback); §3 Task 4.3

questions.stem: Harlow Mutual's repair-invoice schema holds `total_amount` as a number. Garages in Germany and France print totals such as "1.234,50", and on 3% of their invoices the extracted total is off by a factor of 1,000, for example `"total_amount": 1.2345`. The garage's country shows only on the page, in its address and VAT number, not in any metadata. The adjudication system needs one numeric format for each total, but reviewers can't check thousands of euro invoices. Which two changes should the team make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Add normalisation rules to the prompt beside the schema: read the decimal separator from the invoice's country and currency, so "1.234,50" on a euro invoice becomes 1234.50.
options.explanation: The exam guide puts format normalisation rules in the prompt alongside the schema. Only the model sees the page's address, VAT number and currency, so only it can tell which separator is the decimal; a rule tied to country and currency fixes the 3% of misreads at the source.

options.text: Add `currency` and `total_as_printed` fields beside `total_amount`, so that a validator can check each number against the printed string and its currency.
options.explanation: A bare number can't be checked against the page. Keeping the printed string and the currency beside it gives the validator something to compare, so 1.2345 against "1.234,50" fails the check instead of reaching adjudication, without a reviewer reading each euro invoice.

options.text: Add a code step after extraction that rescales `total_amount` for invoices whose garage is in Germany or France, using the country in each document's metadata.
options.explanation: A code step is deterministic, but it needs the country, and the country is only on the page, not in the metadata. Code normalisation suits a value whose format is known from its source, such as a tool's fixed output.

options.text: Change `total_amount` to a string holding the printed value, and let the adjudication system parse each total in its own import step.
options.explanation: Moving the parsing into the adjudication import pushes the locale problem downstream, to a system that expects consistent fields and sees none of the page. A string field suits a value with no single format, not a total that must be a number.

options.text: Have the model return a confidence for `total_amount`, and send each euro invoice whose total scores below 0.9 to the 12 reviewers.
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence is not calibrated, and a model that read a dot as a decimal point is likely to be sure of its mistake. It would also send many correct euro invoices to 12 reviewers who can't take them.

questions.keyConcept: Put format normalisation rules in the prompt beside the schema, and keep the value as printed so a validator can check the conversion.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.3 (normalisation rules in the prompt alongside the schema); §3 Task 4.4 (self-check fields)

questions.stem: Harlow Mutual's validator checks extracted repair invoices against the JSON schema only. An audit finds that 4% of passing records have `repair_date` earlier than the claim's `loss_date`, and in most of them the scan shows the right date: the model misread a smudged digit, such as an 8 read as a 3. These records reach adjudication and are paid or denied on the wrong date. Reviewer time is scarce, while an automatic retry costs one call. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a validator rule that `repair_date` must not precede `loss_date`, and retry each failing record with the scan, the extracted record and that error.
options.explanation: A schema can't see that one date precedes another, so the validator needs the cross-field rule. The right date is on the scan, which makes this a misread a retry can fix: sending the document, the failed record and the specific error lets the model re-read the digit for one call.

options.text: Add a validator rule that `repair_date` must not precede `loss_date`, and send each failing record directly to the 12 reviewers to correct.
options.explanation: The cross-field rule is right, but sending each failure to review spends scarce reviewer time on errors the model can fix by re-reading the scan. Direct review suits failures where the value is absent from the document or a retry has already failed.

options.text: Add a line to the extraction prompt instructing the model to make sure `repair_date` is on or after `loss_date` before it returns a record.
options.explanation: A prompt line may cut the errors, but nothing would detect the ones that remain, and a model asked to make the dates agree without seeing a check may adjust a date to fit. The rule belongs in the validator, where each record is checked.

options.text: Set `repair_date` to null when it precedes `loss_date`, so that a doubtful date stops before adjudication and the record goes on without it.
options.explanation: Nulling the date throws away a value the scan holds and sends adjudication a record with a gap. Null is right when the document lacks the value, not when the model misread it.

questions.keyConcept: Add semantic cross-field checks to the validator, and retry failures with the document, the failed output and the specific error.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.4 (semantic validation, retry with error feedback)

questions.stem: Harlow Mutual wants to move nightly extraction to the Message Batches API for the 50% saving. Today each synchronous extraction calls `lookup_policy` partway through, after reading the document, to fetch the cover limit and excess it needs for `covered_amount`. Each claim reaches the pipeline with its policy number already in the intake record. Results must reach adjudication within 30 hours of the nightly cut-off, and a batch can take up to 24 hours to finish. Which approach should the team use?

options.text: Call `lookup_policy` in code for each claim before submission and add its cover limit and excess to that claim's batch request, so the request finishes in one turn.
options.explanation: A batch request can't make a tool round trip partway through, because a tool result needs a new request. The policy number is known before submission, so code can fetch the limit and excess first and put them in the request; each one then completes in one turn, keeping the 50% saving within one 24-hour round.

options.text: Submit a batch that returns each request's `lookup_policy` call, run the lookups in code, then submit a follow-up batch with the tool results that completes each claim's extraction.
options.explanation: Two rounds do make the tool step possible, but each can take up to 24 hours, so the worst case is 48 hours against a 30-hour deadline. Two rounds suit a deadline with room for both, or a tool input that can't be known before submission.

options.text: Keep nightly extraction on synchronous calls, because a request that needs a tool result partway through can't run inside a batch request.
options.explanation: A batch request can't do a mid-request tool call, but this lookup needn't happen mid-request, since the policy number is known up front. Synchronous calls suit work someone waits on; this nightly job would give up the 50% saving for nothing.

options.text: Submit each claim as one batch request with `tool_choice` forcing `lookup_policy`, so the lookup runs inside the request before the extraction.
options.explanation: Forcing a tool makes the model ask for it; it doesn't run the tool. The batch request would still end with a `tool_use` block, and the result would need a new request. A forced tool suits the first step of a synchronous loop.

questions.keyConcept: A batch request can't do a mid-request tool round trip; fetch what the tool would return beforehand and include it in the request.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 4.5 (no multi-turn tool calling inside a batch request; 24-hour window)

questions.stem: During the nightly run, Harlow Mutual's agent calls `lookup_policyholder("J. Patel", "LE4 7RT")` and gets three matching policyholders at that postcode. The pipeline then picks the one with the newest policy, and an audit found 0.4% of claims attached to the wrong policyholder this way. The run is unattended overnight, so nobody can ask the claimant, but adjudication must not pay the wrong person. What should the agent do when a lookup returns several matches?

options.text: Hold the claim back from adjudication and give the reviewers the three candidates and the missing detail that decides between them, such as a date of birth.
options.explanation: Several matches call for a clarifying identifier, not a heuristic pick. With nobody to ask overnight, the agent hands the decision to a person along with what they need: the three candidates and the identifier that would settle it, so none of the 0.4% are paid to the wrong person.

options.text: Hold the claim back from adjudication and give the reviewers the newest-policy match as the policyholder, so that a reviewer only has to confirm that one match.
options.explanation: It reaches a person, but it hands over only the newest-policy pick, the heuristic behind the 0.4% of errors, without the other two candidates, so the reviewer is steered to confirm a guess. A suggested answer suits a review where the agent's pick rests on a reliable identifier.

options.text: Pick the candidate whose address history fits the claim form best, note in the audit log which identifier would confirm it, and send the claim on to adjudication.
options.explanation: A better-sounding heuristic is still a guess about identity, and logging it doesn't stop a wrong payment. When several people match, get an identifier, or hand the case to a person when nobody can be asked.

options.text: Return an error for the claim and drop it from tonight's run, leaving the claimant to resubmit it later with clearer personal details on the form.
options.explanation: Dropping the claim throws away tonight's work and pushes the problem back to the claimant, when a reviewer could settle it from the candidates. An error return suits a claim that can't be processed at all, not one missing a single identifier.

questions.keyConcept: When a lookup returns several matches, don't pick by heuristic; get a clarifying identifier, or hand the case to a person who can.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.2 (multiple matches need a clarifying identifier)

questions.stem: Harlow Mutual sends a document to review when any field's confidence is below 0.85, one threshold calibrated on the labelled set so the queue fits the 1,800 documents the 12 reviewers check each night. But an analysis of auto-approved documents shows that `claimed_amount` errors cause most overpayments, while 30% of the queue is documents flagged only for `garage_phone`, which adjudication never uses for payment. Reviewer capacity can't grow. How should the routing change?

options.text: Calibrate a threshold per field on the labelled set, stricter for `claimed_amount` and looser for `garage_phone`, keeping the queue within the 1,800 places.
options.explanation: Field-level thresholds calibrated on labelled data route review attention, and with fixed capacity each field's target should follow the cost of its errors. A stricter target for `claimed_amount` and a looser one for `garage_phone` moves the 30% of places spent on phone numbers to the field behind the overpayments.

options.text: Calibrate a threshold per field on the labelled set, each tuned so that its field reaches 99% accuracy, keeping the queue within the 1,800 places.
options.explanation: Per-field calibration is the right mechanism, but one accuracy target for every field treats a wrong phone number like a wrong claimed amount, so places stay spent on `garage_phone`. Equal targets suit fields whose errors cost about the same.

options.text: Calibrate a threshold per document type on the labelled set, stricter for repair invoices than claim forms, keeping the queue within the 1,800 places.
options.explanation: Per-type thresholds can't separate `claimed_amount` from `garage_phone` inside one document, which is where the cost difference lies, so phone-only flags still fill the queue. Calibrating by type suits a document type whose fields are weak across the board.

options.text: Replace the field confidences with one confidence per document from the model, and review the 1,800 lowest-scoring documents each night.
options.explanation: One self-reported score per document is neither calibrated nor tied to a field, so it can't tell a doubtful amount from a doubtful phone number. Model confidence is useful for routing only when calibrated on labelled data, field by field.

questions.keyConcept: With fixed reviewer capacity, calibrate review thresholds per field on labelled data and set stricter targets where an error costs more.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.5 (field-level confidence calibrated on labelled data)

questions.stem: For commercial fleet claims of up to 60 documents, Harlow Mutual's coordinator saves context by summarising earlier documents as it goes, for example "a large March invoice from Dale Motors", and each summary is folded into the next as documents arrive. On these claims, duplicate invoices, where a garage bills one repair twice, now go unnoticed: the summaries no longer hold the amounts or invoice numbers to compare. The coordinator must stay within its context budget. What should the team change?

options.text: Keep a table apart from the running summary, one row per invoice with its number, amount, date and payee, and send that table with each request.
options.explanation: Progressive summarisation turns exact amounts and dates into phrases like "a large March invoice". A table kept outside the summarised history isn't condensed, so each invoice's number, amount, date and payee stay exact and duplicates can be matched, and a row per invoice stays small enough for the budget.

options.text: Keep summarising, but begin each summary with a facts table listing each invoice's number, amount, date and payee, copied from the document.
options.explanation: It uses the right structure in the wrong place: the table sits inside a summary, and each summary is folded into the next, so the table is condensed again with the prose on each pass. Facts that must stay exact belong in a structure kept outside the summarised history.

options.text: Spawn a duplicate-check subagent at the end of each claim that reads the coordinator's summaries, compares the invoices they describe and reports likely duplicates.
options.explanation: A checker that reads the summaries sees only the vague phrases, so it has nothing exact to compare, and the new subagent adds cost without restoring the data. A separate check suits facts that are still there to read.

options.text: Clear the coordinator's history after each block of 20 documents, and start the next block with a fresh context and a short note of the claim number.
options.explanation: Clearing the history throws away the earlier invoices, so a duplicate split across two blocks can't be spotted. Starting fresh suits unrelated work, not a claim whose documents must be compared with each other.

questions.keyConcept: Keep exact transactional facts in a structured block outside summarised history, so repeated summarisation can't blur them.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.1 (case-facts block outside summarised history)

questions.stem: A Harlow Mutual claim has 7 documents. The OCR subagent extracts 6, but a faxed medical bill still fails OCR after the subagent's own two retries, and it returns the 6 records with an error naming that bill. The coordinator then marks the whole claim failed and re-queues all 7 documents for the next night, so the claim loses a day and 6 extractions are paid for twice. The adjudication system scores whatever record it receives. What two changes should the coordinator make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Keep the 6 completed extractions and re-submit only the failed medical bill for extraction, rather than re-queuing the claim's 7 documents for the next night.
options.explanation: One failed document shouldn't throw away six good extractions. Keeping the completed work and retrying only the bill avoids the day's delay and the cost of extracting 6 documents twice.

options.text: If the medical bill still can't be read, flag the claim for a reviewer with a note naming the missing bill, its error and the 6 documents that were extracted.
options.explanation: If the bill still fails, the claim lacks evidence, and adjudication scores whatever it receives, so a person must see it with a note saying what is missing and why. That keeps the partial result honest instead of scoring it as complete.

options.text: Send the claim to `submit_to_adjudication` with the 6 extracted records and leave out the medical bill, since the required fields are already filled.
options.explanation: Filled required fields don't make the evidence complete: adjudication would score a claim missing a medical bill as if it were whole. Partial results can go forward only when the gap is stated and handled.

options.text: Keep marking the claim failed, but re-queue its 7 documents for a run later tonight so that the claim doesn't lose a day.
options.explanation: Re-running sooner shortens the delay but still pays to re-extract the 6 good documents and discards their results. Re-queuing a whole claim suits a failure that affects each document, such as a lost upload.

options.text: Have the OCR subagent pass the failed bill straight to the medical-bill extraction subagent for another attempt, without involving the coordinator.
options.explanation: Subagents handing work to each other route around the coordinator, which then can't track the claim's state or handle the error in one place. The coordinator should decide and route retries of a failed item.

questions.keyConcept: On a partial failure, keep the completed results, retry only what failed, and flag what is still missing rather than restarting.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.3 (partial results, local recovery, propagate what can't be resolved)
